title: Lauren Rose named TCPS Teacher of the Year. Giovanni Wynn is Support Staff of the Year
author: Konner Metz
content:
Lauren Rose named TCPS Teacher of the Year. Giovanni Wynn is Support Staff of the Year

 April 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Lauren Rose and Giovanni Wynn were overcome with emotion Wednesday night when Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi called their names during the district's annual Talbot Stars celebration.Rose, band director at Easton High School, and Wynn, family service coordinator at the St. Michaels Judy Center, were named the 2025-26 Talbot County Public Schools Teacher of the Year and Support Staff of the Year, respectively.
They were showered with hugs and applause from a room full of family, friends and fellow educators at the Easton Elks Lodge.
St. Michaels Elementary School principal Indra Bullock spoke of Wynn's passion and dedication in her role at the Judy Center, a family learning hub designed to prepare children up to 5 years old and their families for early education.
"She understands the unique challenges that each family faces and tailors her support to meet their specific needs," Bullock said. "Her compassionate nature allows her to build strong and trusting relationships with both parents and children, as well as staff, making them feel valued and understood."
In addition to Wynn, the finalists for Support Staff of the Year honored Wednesday included: Stacie Rice, special education secretary at Easton Middle; Jane Tillman, math and reading interventionist at Chapel District Elementary; and Christina Titz, instructional assistant at Easton Middle.
Rose was honored by Easton High School principal Sherry Spurry, who read aloud a student's nomination of Rose for the Teacher of the Year award.
"Mrs. Rose has a unique ability to transform the band room into a place where students feel safe, supported and encouraged to grow," the nomination read. "Whether it's a new decoration on the walls or a thoughtful conversation with a student, she makes the space her own, turning it into a welcoming environment for all of us."
The nomination stated Rose has been integral in facilitating band fundraisers and advocating for the band to be centrally located in the stands at Easton High football games.
"Mrs. Rose has been a guiding force in my own development," the student's nomination continued. "She has helped me overcome self-doubt, and has always been there to offer guidance during challenging times. Mrs. Rose's love for her students and her dedication to making our school a better place are truly inspiring."
Rose was one of four finalists for Teacher of the Year, alongside Rebecca Phillips, kindergarten teacher at Chapel District Elementary; Kathy Regan, third grade teacher at St. Michaels Elementary; and Holly Sump, kindergarten teacher at Chapel District Elementary.
Helga Einhorn, assistant superintendent of school leadership and student success, thanked the teachers for their hard work in the demanding field of education.
"Each of you exemplified the best of our profession, a profession that really is fraught with challenges, even on the best of days," Einhorn said. "Despite this, each one of you enter your schools and your classroom each day only seeing opportunities."
Board of Education President Emily Jackson said the staff and teacher finalists are life changers, motivators and inspirations.
"To all of our nominees, tonight is for you," Jackson said. "Thank you for everything you do, and I hope you feel celebrated and appreciated and seen for your unique and outstanding contribution."

title: Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Calvert County School Board member Melissa Goshorn's comment at the panel's April meeting proved to be prophetic."I recognize it's going to make a lot of people unhappy," Goshorn said just prior to requesting that Superintendent of Schools Andraé Townsel to remove "Safe Space" stickers from school buildings.
Goshorn based her request on anecdotal information she received at a National School Boards Association conference during what she described as a "bone-chilling session" presented by the Beau Biden Foundation.
The story relayed to session attendees dealt with a principal who was arrested on child sex abuse charges and may have gained children's confidence by having a "Safe Space" sticker on the office door.
The sticker is widely used as a sign that LGBTQ students will not be discriminated in that space.
"I think we need to have them removed," Goshorn said.
School maintenance staff removed the stickers and the predicted unhappiness manifested itself during the board's May 8 meeting when 19 of the 20 speakers addressed the issue during the public comment segment. While a handful of the speakers indicated support for the sticker removal, many expressed opposition.
Sheri Tardio of Prince Frederick called the issue "manufactured outrage. Safe space stickers do not promote ideology. Diversity is a fact."
"You are not hiding your biases very well," said Stacy Tayman, president of the Calvert Association for Educational Support Staff.
"Removing stickers is not a violation of First Amendment rights," said school board President Jana Post in her closing comments, adding that the April discussion "was twisted" into an LGBTQ issue.
"Real safety comes from a culture of trust," Post said.
At the conclusion of public comments, board member Paul Harrison made a motion to discuss "a flag policy" at a future meeting. That policy would likely be aimed at setting parameters for displays of flags, posters and decals in school buildings. The motion passed unanimously.
Supervisor's post
The school board unanimously approved the appointment of Marc Watson as supervisor of health, physical education and athletics. The Indiana University of Pennsylvania graduate is a familiar face in Calvert County where he has previously served as a teacher, coach and principal.
Most recently, Watson served as principal of King George High School in Virginia.
Watson told the board he was looking forward to "continuing to create this wonderful environment of learning and athletics" in Calvert County.
In recommending Watson for the appointment, Townsel said the returning administrator will provide "training and mentorship for coaches."

title: How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore

 March 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Delegate Jay Jacobs, who represents Maryland's District 36 — encompassing Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline counties — has seen the region through economic peaks and valleys. But the COVID-19 pandemic presented a crisis unlike any other.At the same time, it brought a rare opportunity.
Through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), Maryland received $3.7 billion in federal relief funds. Jacobs estimated that roughly $88 million of that flowed into his district over the past five years.
"The money gave counties and municipalities a chance to get things done when they normally might not have had that opportunity," Jacobs said.
Across the district, more than 200 projects were funded through ARPA, aimed at bolstering local infrastructure, supporting nonprofits and modernizing essential services.
Rock Hall to Queen Anne's: Local Needs, Local SolutionsEach town took a unique approach, reflecting ARPA's flexible framework.
In Rock Hall, the town's aging wastewater system was a priority. Mayor James Cook said of the $1.3 million received, $300,000 went toward replacing the headworks at the sewer plant — a key filter that removes debris such as grease and rags from wastewater.
Chestertown formed a task force led by Ward 2 Council member Tom Herz to ensure transparency and community input. Of the $4.25 million allocated, local nonprofits were invited to align funding requests with the town's comprehensive plan.
In Galena, $570,000 supported road improvements designed to make parks more accessible and attract visitors.
Betterton directed its $311,000 toward modernizing its website to be ADA-compliant, enabling online payments, purchasing an air purifying unit, and upgrading pump stations with generators for resilience.
Millington received $504,821, though specific projects were not detailed.
Queen Anne's County saw one of the largest allocations: $16.3 million. Projects included installing 3,300 feet of water line at the Old Towne Shopping Center, investing $900,000 to upgrade affordable housing units, and expanding broadband access with $1.5 million. Six new consoles were also added to the county's 911 backup center, and cell phone boosters were installed in public schools to strengthen communication in rural areas.
Countywide Efforts and Broadband ExpansionIn Cecil County, where municipalities received a greater share of ARPA funds than the county itself, a major initiative focused on expanding high-speed internet. A $16.2 million broadband project combined $12.8 million in state funds, $2.5 million from internet service providers, and $900,000 in ARPA funds contributed by the county.
According to county officials, additional ARPA investments went toward two emergency medical services paramedic stations and a new training center for the Cecil County Sheriff's Office.
Rising Sun used $2,300 for infrastructure repairs, while the Town of North East applied its share to enhance police department operations.
In Caroline County, which received just under $6.5 million, part of the funding was used for infrastructure, while a portion supported reentry programs and post-release case management for individuals leaving the Ordnance Road Detention Facility.
Jacobs noted that ARPA's flexibility was one of its most valuable aspects.
"It was not one size fits all," he said. "Municipalities could use the money to meet their specific needs — with the only caveat being it must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026."
As ARPA Winds Down, Financial Pressure MountsNow, with the funding window closing, local governments are bracing for its absence. Jacobs said the drying up of ARPA funds is intensifying pressure on the state as the General Assembly works to pass the FY 2026 budget — which currently faces a $3.5 billion shortfall.
"Certain services were being relied on and now are cut off," Jacobs said. "ARPA funds possibly would have kept some of these programs afloat."
A notable cut is the reduction in senior care funding by the Maryland Department of Aging. Jacobs said the proposed $2.5 million budget — an 18% reduction — could translate to about $28,000 less per county. He warned this could destabilize staffing and services for vulnerable seniors, such as in-home care, transportation and meal delivery.
"These cuts will be felt, not by the lawmakers, but by ordinary hardworking folks who have to make decisions about affording food or putting gas in the car," he said.
Talbot County: Planning for LongevityTalbot County took a strategic approach. Officials distributed surveys to identify community priorities, which included broadband access, public health, and household assistance.
According to Cassandra Vanhooser, director of Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism, the county received about $7.2 million in ARPA funds. The goal, she said, was to ensure that projects wouldn't falter once federal dollars were gone.
"These are largely capital items, these are one-time items... a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," said then Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher. "We need to be very careful about how this is done."
Among Talbot's allocations:
- $1.75 million to Easton Utilities' Connect Talbot project to expand broadband to rural residents.
- $105,000 to the Chesapeake Center in Easton to replace a failing septic system and connect to county sewer.
- $500,000 in grants for volunteer fire company equipment upgrades.
"People recognize that this is transformational money," Vanhooser said at the time of the funding discussion, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be a driving force for change and to impact the lives of our citizens."
Looking AheadAs the Dec. 31, 2024 obligation deadline nears, and the Dec. 31, 2026 expenditure deadline looms, local leaders are focused on maximizing remaining funds while grappling with what comes next.
Jacobs is urging urgency from lawmakers.
"With less than 20 days in session," he said, "the Assembly needs to come up with solutions — and fast."

title: Homemade cleaning solutions save money
author: Mary Hunt
content:
Homemade cleaning solutions save money

 August 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Hunt | Page: A6 | Section: News 
 
 268
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I pretty much hate to buy things I know I can make for less money and in a fraction of the time it takes to find them in a store.Take cleaning products, for example.Knowing I can make specific cleaners for pennies that cost dollars in a store just makes me happy. It's a no-brainer.Here are my top handy recipes to help you get started saving all that money you've been spending on cleaners:EYEGLASSES CLEANING SOLUTIONFill a spray bottle of any size 3/4 full with 70 percent isopropyl rubbing alcohol (91 or 99 percent are fine to use but more costly and not necessary).Add 2 small drops of mild dishwashing liquid (Blue Dawn is ideal), and fill the rest of the bottle with distilled water (see note).Add the spray top, and gently shake the bottle by rolling it between your hands or on a countertop, so as to not create a lot of bubbles. To use: Spray both sides of your lenses, and gently rub them clean with a clean microfiber cloth.WINDSHIELD WASHER FLUIDPour 3 cups rubbing alcohol, 1 tablespoon Blue Dawn and 10 cups distilled water into a 1-gallon plastic jug. Shake thoroughly to mix. Pour into your car windshield washer reservoir in place of commercial windshield washer fluid. Always shake prior to adding to the reservoir.The alcohol speeds the drying time and prevents the windows from freezing or cracking in the winter.Mary Hunt invites you to visit her at Everyday-Cheapskate.com, where this column is archived complete with links and resources for all recommended products and services. title: Five counties unite for recovery awareness event at Church Hill Park
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Five counties unite for recovery awareness event at Church Hill Park

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 534
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH HILL — Standing united as one community in support of recovery and awareness across the area, Mid Shore Behavioral Health, Inc. hosted its annual five county collaborative Going Purple Together at Church Hill Park Sept. 27.Organizations and agencies from neighboring counties of Queen Anne's, Talbot, Kent Caroline, and Dorchester came together to show the community all the resources available for substance recovery, mental health, addiction, and support.
Annually supporting recovery across the Mid-Shore region, the 2025 Going Purple Together event offered a blend of, fun, education and community engagement, with local vendors, activities, and the message of continually learning about substance abuse, overdose, recovery, peer support, and prevention.
Highlighting important community resources in a fun, casual environment, festivities were complete with DJ, food trucks, giveaways, family fun activities and performances by Hula Hoop Love.
Building awareness through engagement
Recognizing substance abuse awareness and prevention is more nuanced than "Just Say No" community engagement is the first step in addressing issues.
By building awareness in a fun environment, the community can be proactive and not reactive, said Queen Anne's County Circuit Court Judge Lynn Knight, a founder of the Queen Anne's County Circuit Court Assisted Recovery and Treatment program.
Ten years ago substance abuse resources did not exist in the county like they do today, and the growth in support is tremendous, she said.
Personal stories of recovery
Showcasing the possibilities of recovery straight from those who have lived it first hand, peer support specialists shared their personal experiences to help inspire and encourage those in need.
One such peer, Kaylee Whitby, of Federalsburg, noted for the longest time her personal story was a continual cycle riddled with active addiction, treatment, jail, and legal issues.
Finally after an attempt on her own life, Whitby fought to give herself a new way of living because "it was obvious my way was not working."
Through continual effort and the support of peers, Whitby was able to join in recovery services that finally made a lasting impact on her recovery journey and ultimately her life.
Whitby voiced gratitude for the opportunities offered through supportive recovery houses, including security, accountability, growth, and networking connections still part of her life today.
"Recovery saved my life," she said. Because of recovery Whitby learned to surrender and make amends to rebuild relationships. Whitby was able to be the mother that her children deserved and be the person she wanted to be.
Knowing there were others out in the community with their own similar experiences helped shape Whitby and she was eager to pay that forward to inspire others and be part of that journey.
"Today I chose to live," Whitby said.
Comprehensive support services
Understanding the many avenues that go hand in hand with recovery, organizations connected the community with the tools for support including behavioral and mental health, social services, gambling help, out and inpatient services, as well as resources for loved ones of those facing diseases of addiction.
Mid Shore Behavioral Health, is proud to continually work closely with community and county health departments and administration to erase stigma and further advocacy said Alisha Saulsbury, forensic mental health program manager.
Seeing people smile proud of themselves on their recovery journey makes it all worthwhile, Saulsbury said.
More information about Mid Shore Behavioral Health can be found at midshorebehavioralhealth.org.

title: Donald F. Johnson
content:
Donald F. Johnson

 October 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 8 | Section: News

 CAMBRIDGE - The Honorable Donald F. Johnson, 80, of Cambridge peacefully went home to be with Jesus on Saturday, October 14, 2023. He was born on December 6, 1942, in Cambridge, Maryland to the late Arthur N. Johnson and Emma (Parks) Johnson Moore.Donald graduated from Cambridge High School, Class of 1960. He earned his B.S. in 1964 from Salisbury State College and his J.D. in 1969 from University of Baltimore School of Law. He was the Assistant States Attorney for Anne Arundel and Dorchester Counties from 1969-1974. Then he entered private practice until he was appointed Circuit Court Judge for Dorchester County in 1984. During his 20 years serving as the County Administrative Judge for the 1st Judicial Circuit, he was a panel chair for the Health Claims Arbitration Board and a member of the Attorney Grievance Commission. He was a past president of the Rotary Club of Cambridge and on the Board of Directors for the Dorchester General Hospital. He was a member of Grace Methodist Church, Rotary Club, Dorchester Historical Society, Barcca Class, Maryland Bar Association and Dorchester County Bar Association. He enjoyed sailing, woodworking, traveling, spending time with his family, antiquing, and visiting historical sites.He is survived by his wife of 58 years, Joan Shimer Johnson of Cambridge, a daughter Emmajane Olinde and husband Greg of Fruitland, a son Donald F. Johnson, Jr. and wife Amy Dukes of Wilmington, NC, three grandchildren Grace Olinde, Victoria Olinde and Mason Olinde and fiancée Brooke Planner, two brothers Wayne A. Johnson and wife Donna of Cambridge and Jeffrey L. Johnson of Salisbury, and numerous nieces and nephews.A Celebration of Life will be held on Wednesday, October 25, 2023 at 10:30am at Grace Methodist Church with Rev. title: Historical Society relationship and Regional Detention Center update
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Historical Society relationship and Regional Detention Center update

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 389
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Historical Society wants to rebuild a working relationship with the County Commissioners so they can get some help funding for different projects to help bring tourist to the town."We have in and around Preston a five-mile radius the most significant components of the Underground Railroad in the United States," lifetime member of the historical society Mick McCrea said.
The Linchester Mill historical sight offers many trials and buildings to where Harriet Tubman and other prominent individuals lived.
"We have actual buildings you can literally walk in the footsteps of people where they stayed in the homes where they got freedom from," McCrea said.
Another suggestion made by historical society board member David "Gene" Harris that the Linchester Mill pond be restored for many reasons.
"If we ever had a major fire, the Linchester Mill pond would be an ideal spot to recharge their fire trucks," Harris said.
The County Commissioners want to establish a working relationship as well, a big component is funding and both sides will plan to work together in the future to help with the Linchester historical sight.
Potential Regional Detention Center updateThe potential Regional Detention Center came up in discussion again for the commissioners.
The center would be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill and would house detainees from Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties. It aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
The commissioners said they still have not received exact numbers for how much everything will cost and how much the county will save by joining the agreement with the other counties.
Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested that the county should do an independent evaluation of the operating cost.
"This decision is going to depend on the operational cost and I'm talking long range operational cost," Porter said. "Would it make sense for us to engage someone to do an independent evaluation of these operating cost?"
The county also want numbers crunched on transportation, employment and other things.
"The biggest question we all have is the operating side of the detention center," Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said.
The county will have Fox run an independent evaluation to get some calculated numbers to the administrators.

title: Easton man pleads guilty to possessing child pornography
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton man pleads guilty to possessing child pornography

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 385
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An Easton man pleaded guilty to four counts of possession of child pornography during a plea hearing on Thursday in the Talbot County Circuit Court.In June, Travis Schwaninger, 43, was arrested on eight counts of possessing child pornography following the execution of a search warrant where detectives from the Talbot County Sheriff's Office found evidence of child pornography on Schwaninger's electronic devices.
Before his arrest, the Easton Police Department Criminal Investigations Unit had received several tips about Schwaninger from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
On Thursday, Maryland Circuit Court Judge Theresa Adams suspended all of the five-year sentences for each of the four counts Schwaninger pleaded guilty to. This means he will serve no jail time.
Adams said Schwaninger will have to serve five years of supervised probation, register as a Tier I sex offender and submit to supervision, meaning that he will have to comply with a sex offender management program.
The state agreed not to prosecute the remaining four charges Schwaninger faced.
Before handing down Schwaninger's sentence, Adams said that by obtaining and possessing the videos, Schwaninger was participating in the child pornography industry.
"The most important thing we can all do is protect children," she said.
During the plea hearing, Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale gave descriptions of the four videos that Schwaninger pleaded guilty to having. He said the children in the videos were real children, not created by artificial intelligence.
Coale said that although Schwaninger had not manufactured the videos, his "participation in that market allows the market to flourish."
Schwaninger's attorney Thomas Maronick Jr. said his client "looked at some pictures he should not have" and didn't distribute them. Maronick said Schwaninger has since met with a counselor experienced in treating sex offenders. Maronick said the counselor did not feel that Schwaninger had a problem that requires "lengthy" therapy.
This was "a crime of curiosity," Maronick said, later adding that Schwaninger didn't realize the industry he was supporting.
Schwaninger told Adams that he came across the videos on social media toward the end of 2023.
"It was like watching a train wreck," he said about the videos. "I know better."
Schwaninger said the videos were on an old phone and didn't realize they were on the phone he was using at the time of his arrest. He said he thought he had deleted the videos.

title: Lions tighten their grip on North
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Lions tighten their grip on North

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 754
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Noah Palmer offered somewhat of an explanation for his latest victory."My curveball," Queen Anne's County High's senior right-hander said with a game-winning smile. "I don't know what to say. I haven't been throwing it all year. It's been iffy. But I came out of the gate and it came out of my hand amazingly. And I was able to throw a split-finger today amazingly, too. I just threw it and it hit spots. That's all I got to say."
Palmer didn't have to say much more late Tuesday afternoon, as he yielded five hits in six-plus innings to help Queen Anne's to an 11-8 victory over Easton, drawing the Lions closer to their first North Bayside title since 1980.
Winners of five straight, Queen Anne's (8-6 overall, 5-1 North Bayside) can clinch the North championship with victories over Cambridge-South Dorchester and Kent County.
Colonel Richardson (11-5, 5-2), which blanked St. Michaels 3-0 yesterday behind Jordan Regulski's complete-game three-hitter, still remains in contention in the North. Should the Lions lose one of their two remaining division contests and finish tied with Colonel, the Colonels would win the North via their 8-1 victory over Queen Anne's in the only head-to-head meeting between the two schools this season.
Kent Island (7-8, 5-2) also has an outside shot. Though they lost to Queen Anne's in the second meeting between the two schools — which counts toward the division standings — the Bucs defeated Colonel and hold the tiebreaker between those two schools.
Easton (10-5, 4-3), which was in the running for its first North crown since 2007, got two first-inning runs against Palmer (5-2) but then was held scoreless by the Lions ace until the bottom of the sixth inning.
"Credit goes to their pitcher," Easton head coach Albert Pritchett said of Palmer, who struck out six and walked two before being relieved in the seventh. "He did a great job. After the first couple of innings he really settled in, working on his pitches, threw strikes."
Palmer and Easton's Kayden Webb (4-1) were locked in a pitcher's duel, tied at 2-2 heading to the top of the sixth.
That's when the Lions busted the game open, scoring six runs on five hits.
With one out, Noah Cramer walked, moved to second on a low pitch and scored the go-ahead run on Chance Hegedus' double down the left-field line. Ethan Keppler singled, sending Hegedus (3 for 4, three runs) to third. Hegedus got caught in a rundown between home and third. Warrior catcher Colin Mooney ran Hegedus back before throwing the ball to third baseman Garrett Fink. But with no one covering home, Hegedus raced across the plate for a 4-2 lead.
Webb was relieved after Brendan Parsley singled. Dustin Blue walked the first man he faced before Travis Sutch (4 for 4, three RBIs), whose solo homer off the left-field pole tied the game at 2-2 in the third, singled through the right side, plating two runs for a 6-2 lead. Two batters later, Dulin Clark belted a two-run double for an 8-2 lead.
"I think we're hitting pretty good right now," Travis Sutch said. "Definitely a big improvement over the last couple games. Everybody's starting to get going now, especially the bottom of our lineup."
Easton ended its scoring drought in the bottom of the sixth. Dylan Cassell doubled and scored when Blue sent a shot over Parsley's head in center field. Chase Raab's sacrifice fly made it 8-4. But Palmer got a strikeout and groundout to end the inning.
"He did a great job today," Queen Anne's head coach Rick Sutch said of Palmer. "He knew this was a big game. We went into it knowing that we were in the driver's seat as far as the Bayside North. He knew how big this was and he had at least five days off, so he was fresh.
"Usually Noah doesn't let anything bother him so once he got the lead I wasn't really too concerned," Coach Sutch added. "Webb's a good pitcher on the other side, so we knew we had to get to him early to get to the bullpen. But Noah did a great job. He controlled the game."
Queen Anne's tacked on three runs on five hits in the seventh, stretching their lead to 11-4.
The Warriors pieced together their biggest inning in the seventh, with Mikey O'Connor hitting a two-run single and Carter Mooney sending a sacrifice fly to center to make it 11-8 before Clough induced a game-ending groundout.
Notes: Webb tripled in the first and Colin Mooney doubled in the seventh for Easton.

title: Mobsters, spies, anarchists, Klan members - and Trump - Prosecutors use racketeering, spy and Reconstruction laws in Trump criminal indictments
content:
Mobsters, spies, anarchists, Klan members - and Trump - Prosecutors use racketeering, spy and Reconstruction laws in Trump criminal indictments

 August 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A2 | Section: News 
 
 911
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Former president Donald Trump has been charged like mobster and drug kingpin in Georgia, like an anarchist and foreign spy in Florida and like a post-Civil War Ku Klux Klan member in Washington D.C. as he faces now a quartet of criminal charges in the run-up to 2024 election.Trump was indicted by a Fulton County, Georgia grand jury along with 2024 campaign cohorts and attorneys - including Rudy Giuliani, Jenna Ellis and White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows - over attempts to reverse President Joe Biden's 11,779-vote win in the Peach State.Part of that indictment includes racketeering charges conventionally used against organized crime syndicates and criminal gangs."The indictment alleges that rather than abide by Georgia's legal process for election challenges, the defendants engaged in a criminal racketeering enterprise to overturn Georgia's presidential election result," Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, a Democrat, said during a late-night news conference Monday, Aug. 14, announcing the indictment of the former president and leading 2024 GOP White House candidate.The indictment includes RICO (Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations), making false statements and other election meddling charges. The criminal charges to making false statements, like some of other federal allegations against Trump, will face First Amendment free speech counterarguments.Across the U.S., RICO cases have commonly been used against organized crime syndicates and criminal gangs including John Gotti's Gambino Crime Family, the Hells Angels, Latin Kings and the Cowboy Mafia, which used shrimp boats to smuggle illegal marijuana in the late 1970. There have been RICO charges used in some corporate and other corruption cases including 2022 indictments of some current and former soccer officials associated with FIFA and CONCACAF.In Georgia, RICO convictions could potentially bring prison terms of 5 to 20 years.According to the Associated Press, the Trump indictment includes criminal charges related to "attempting to persuade Georgia lawmakers to ignore the will of voters and appoint a new slate of electoral college electors favorable to Trump." "In one particularly brazen episode, it also outlines a plot involving one of his lawyers to access voting machines in a rural Georgia county and steal data from a voting machine company," the AP writes.Like with his federal indictments and charges in New York of filing false business claims to cover up alleged hush money paid to porn star Stormy Daniels and Playboy model, Karen McDougal, Trump lambasted the charges as politically motivated falsehoods aimed to undermining his 2024 White House bid."Can you believe it? This failed District Attorney from Atlanta, Fani Willis, where murders and other violent crime soars daily to new record highs, is charging me with 2020 Presidential Election Interference. No, Fani, the only Election Interference was done by those that Rigged and Stole the Election," Trump said in a statement on social media platform Truth Social. "Those are the ones you should be going after, not the innocent people that are fighting for Election Integrity!" Ellis and Guiliani, who served as Trump campaign lawyers, say they are being charged criminally for providing legal advice. "The Democrats and the Fulton County DA are criminalizing the practice of law," Ellis said in a social media statement.U.S. Justice Department Special Prosecutor Jack Smith has invoked federal grand juries in Florida and D.C. to indict Trump via the 1917 Espionage Act over his alleged misappropriation of classified documents and a post-Civil War law aimed at violent harassment by the Ku Klux Klan over the Jan. 6 Capitol riot and efforts to derail Congress' certification of Biden as the 2020 election winner.The Espionage Act has been previously used against Julian Assange, Edward Snowden, Julius and Ethen Rosenbereg and early 20th Century anarchist writer Emma Goldman.All told, Trump, 77, could potentially be jailed for the rest of his life if convicted and sentenced aggressively by state and federal judges.Tung Yin, a law professor at Lewis & Clark Law School in Portland, Oregon, said jury selections will be very important in the cases against Trump and prospective jurors may hide their love, disdain or other views toward the former Republican president."That person might give very bland answers during jury selection," XXX said. "It would be very hard to ferratt someone like this out. you get one person out of 12 you have a hung jury." The timing of the trials could run into and potentially after the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign elections.Yin sees the classified documents case where Trump is accused of improperly taking classified materials from the White House to his Florida estate as the stronger of the federal prosecutions.If convicted, Trump, the leading opposition candidate currently to President Biden, could potentially be jailed.For example, Jan. 6th charges in D.C. (which Biden won over Trump 92% to 5%) could result in Trump going to a federal prison for between 57 to 71 months, according to an estimate from Yin. That's between just under four and almost six years.Politically, as expected, Trump-aligned Republicans criticized the Georgia indictment while Democrats and progressives hailed the effort to convict and potentially imprison the bombastic populist former president.

title: Brutal treatment of beautiful field
content:
Brutal treatment of beautiful field

 I live in the Greens at Cross Court. Across from the entrance to the complex is an open field about the size of a football field.For most of the years that we have lived here that field was left in its natural state. That meant lots of wild flowers (chicory, daisies, black-eyed Susans, Queen Anne's lace, Joe Pye, milkweed, etc.).Also birds were among the inhabitants, especially redwing blackbirds, as well as many butterflies (swallowtails, monarchs, buckeyes, fritillaries, cabbage whites, blues, morning cloaks).Now twice a year it is mowed down to an ugly field of clumps of vegetation.And why? So I can see the bypass.To destroy such a natural magnet for native flowers, butterflies and birds makes a mockery of leadership that professes to care about the environment.My question is: What government agencies make this decision - town, county or state? I want the responsible government entity to be aware of the unhappiness that this brutal treatment of a formerly beautiful field has caused.JAMES CARROLL Easton

title: Dems score coup with McCarthy ouster
author: David Harsanyi
content:
Dems score coup with McCarthy ouster

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: David Harsanyi | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 640
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kevin McCarthy has become the first House speaker to ever be successfully ousted in a motion to vacate vote. One day, you can tell your grandchildren you were alive to witness this completely pointless bit of history.Rep. Matt Gaetz's (R-Fla.) self-aggrandizing political stunt makes no sense and changes nothing - other than perhaps his fundraising totals.And other than some platitudinous blathering about "the establishment" and "the uniparty," I still haven't seen anyone offer a coherent reason - not even retroactively - for how any of this is the "best way to advance the conservative agenda." It would be one thing, perhaps an admirable thing, if Gaetz had gone on this crusade for a coherent ideological or principled reason. But his post-ousting demagoguery and grandstanding about issues completely unrelated to McCarthy's job performance proved it was a personal matter."I don't think voting against Kevin McCarthy is chaos," Gaetz explained."I think $33 trillion in debt is chaos. I think that facing a $2.2 trillion annual deficit is chaos." Now, there are numerous people to blame for the impending fiscal disaster, but McCarthy is no more guilty than most.One of the least convincing claims by Gaetz's defenders is that McCarthy was punished for ignoring the base. "The base," of course, is a popular euphemism for the most vociferous populist faction of the GOP.This faction enjoys blowing things up - mostly their own party's prospects. In this case, the "base" was represented by eight Republicans and the entire Democratic Party.And among these principled eight GOPers who were fighting for the honor of the base - what The New York Times called the "far-right GOP faction" - were Reps.Nancy Mace (who said Gaetz was a "fraud" the last time he tried to knock off McCarthy) and Ken Buck (who we last heard was reportedly looking for a CNN gig). I'm going to go out on a limb and say that the future of conservatism was not the motivating factor for their votes.Most Trump-endorsed candidates didn't even participate in McCarthy's removal. Donald Trump himself tepidly supported the speaker because, as he noted, the man had said "very great things" about him. And, really, what's more important? Though, I bet McCarthy was expecting a far more energetic defense after pathetically ingratiating himself to the former president a couple of weeks ago.Even if Gaetz had excellent reasons, Republicans did not eject McCarthy.Eight Republicans can't do anything by themselves. No, 208 Democrats ousted McCarthy with the help of some petulant backbenchers nursing personal vendettas. It is a political coup for the Dems.Gaetz, who only yesterday was going on about McCarthy's "secret deal" with Democrats, had no qualms sitting on the opposition side of the House plotting to oust a speaker who holds a rickety nine-seat majority. If there was actually a brewing House rebellion, Gaetz would have been able to corral far more votes.But Gaetz wanted to "break the fever" of D.C., so he teamed up with minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, "the squad," Adam Schiff and so on. Jeffries claimed he was supporting Gaetz's efforts because Republicans have shown an "unwillingness to break from MAGA extremism in an authentic and comprehensive manner." The notion that Democrats are backing a leading MAGA loyalist because they want to temper the "extremism" of Republicans makes about as much sense as Jamaal Bowman's fire alarm story. Democrats keep pretending they yearn for a more responsible GOP and stable political environment, then keep supporting every fringe effort and candidate to undermine both.Of course, no one is owed anything.McCarthy isn't the only person available in D.C. to serve as a middling speaker of the House. And, frankly, if he'd been more talented at the job, he might have headed off this challenge more effectively. But it's doubtful anyone is going to perform better with a slender majority and the Senate and presidency in Democrats' hands.But then again, none of that matters when you're having a tantrum.

title: Cambridge man urges water caution after 'flesh-eating bacteria' infection
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge man urges water caution after 'flesh-eating bacteria' infection

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 942
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Facing a life-altering bacterial infection from the local river, a local couple is urging the community to be more informed swimmers.A typical day at the shore turned a couple's lives upside down after a sharp step opened a wound on a man's leg and exposed him to bacteria in the Chester River last summer.
For over a year, Kyle "Slade" Register, of Cambridge has been fighting Vibrio, a "flesh-eating" bacteria found in local rivers.
Register and Audra Williamson were swimming in the Chester River on Aug. 16, 2024 when Register stepped on what they presume was a sharp oyster shell and cut a small, deep gash on the inside of Register's left foot. The couple quickly went to work cleaning the wound with peroxide and rubbing alcohol and scrubbed it with antibacterial soap before wrapping it.
Going to bed as normal, "We never dreamt we would wake up the next morning to his foot being the size of a bowling pin with a red streak starting up his leg," Williamson said.
Register spent a week at the hospital in Easton before being transferred to University of Maryland Shock Trauma, where he stayed for the following month. While there, Register had four surgeries to save his leg.
"It's been a year, and he is still going to wound care twice a week," Williamson said.
Register is unable to work full-time with the wound, as the two-inch gash ended in the entire inside of his left calf and the inside of his left foot being cut out, with a wound vac attached for months.
The couple went from having a "pretty normal life," to losing work and having their lives turned upside down, Williamson said.
Now beginning to get back on their feet, the two are sharing their story as a precautionary tale to others taking a dip.
"We just want to prevent this from happening to others," Williamson said.
According to the U.S Environmental Protection Agency, Vibrio are naturally occurring bacteria found in brackish environments like the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries, such as the Chester River. In rare cases, swimmers can develop illnesses or infections if an open wound is exposed to polluted water.
A "tough construction worker type," who never thought twice about what was hidden in waterways, Register said his entire view of the water changed after that incident.
A "fish," all his life, Register now looks at the water with "abject sadness."
Taking it one day at a time, the Cambridge couple still drive around the Chesapeake Bay, estuaries, and areas like Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge to look at the water "but I don't go in," Register said.
Looking back on the treatment and recovery he has faced and the journey still to come, "I don't want a parent to feel that pain," Register said and seeks to share his story with others.
Not to scare people, but to help them understand the possibilities, Register said. "The public needs to be more educated about this," he said.
Williamson encouraged checking out the local environmental organizations information and the EPA website before swimming or boating.
Register welcomes the opportunities to share his story and can be reached at sladeregister81@gmail.com.
According to Shorerivers' Swimmable ShoreRivers Bacteria Monitoring Program Report, "Is it safe to swim in the river?" is one of the most common questions Riverkeepers hear from community members. There are inherent risks with coming in contact with water in a living estuary, and ShoreRivers works to understand the bacterial levels associated with enterococci, an EPA recommended indicator for human health risks.
Enterococci includes more than 17 species of fecal bacteria and is found in the intestines of warm-blooded animals. High levels of enterococci can indicate elevated risks for human contact with pathogens and other bacteria, such as E-coli. While there are natural bacteria levels in local rivers due to wildlife and decomposition, there are also pollution sources such as failing septic systems and faulty sewer lines, pet waste, mishandling of boat waste, and some organic fertilizers that can pose threats to human health.
"There are additional risks with open water swimming that we do not regularly monitor, including vibrio, toxic algal blooms, and other biological and chemical toxins," according to the report.
ShoreRivers' seasonal bacteria monitoring program regularly monitors nearly 50 sites where people frequently come in contact with water, including popular swimming locations, marinas, yacht clubs, and towns. Swim Tester volunteers collect water samples every Thursday morning from Memorial Day to Labor Day. Riverkeepers then analyze the samples and distribute data on bacteria levels in the river, aiming to provide the public with the information needed to make educated decisions about their contact with the water.
The Swimmable ShoreRivers program utilizes the standardized EPA criteria for recreational swimming of 104 Colony Forming Units (CFU)/100ml for analyzing a single bacteria sample. Anything equal to or higher than 104 CFU is a failing sample, and anything below 104 CFU is a passing sample. Not all test sites are designated swimming areas.
According to Shore Rivers, bacteria levels can change, particularly as a result of significant rain events.
ShoreRivers always recommends following best practices when recreating in local waterways including rinsing off after swimming, avoiding swimming for 24–48 hours after a rain event, and staying out of the water with open cuts or wounds to minimize exposure to potentially harmful bacteria.
As part of its ongoing work to protect and restore local rivers and creeks, ShoreRivers weekly bacteria monitoring reports are posted every Friday from Memorial Day to Labor Day at www.shorerivers.org/swim.
Though the seasonal Swimmable ShoreRivers testing has wrapped up for this year, a full report on each regularly monitored site is expected in October.
Information on how to prevent and respond to possible infections, can be found in the Maryland Department of the Environment.

title: Preston man sentenced to 15 years for stabbing
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Preston man sentenced to 15 years for stabbing

 February 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — A Preston man was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison for the February 2022 stabbing of a then 25-year-old woman.Agreeing with a recommendation from the prosecution, Caroline County Circuit Judge Heather Price handed Mark William Thompkins a 30-year sentence with all but 15 years suspended. He will receive credit for 714 days, or nearly two years, already served, according to court records.
Thompkins, 26, pleaded guilty last October to one count of attempted second-degree murder.
Price also referred Thompkins to the Patuxent Institution, a treatment-oriented, maximum security correctional facility.
"I believe that it was an appropriate sentence," said Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin, who prosecuted the case. "Unfortunately, the mental health system is broken and failed both the victim and Mr. Thompkins."
Thompkins' defense attorney, Jesse Hicks, could not be reached for comment.
Thursday's sentence comes nearly two years after the young woman was stabbed near Holly Park Drive and Gilpin Point Road in Preston shortly before 3 p.m. on Feb. 17, 2022.
During the Oct. 30 plea hearing, Franklin said trash collection workers near the scene first saw the woman sitting in the driver's seat of her vehicle with a man, later identified as Thompkins, seated behind her.
Thompkins began striking the woman with his fists, then brandished a knife to stab her neck.
The woman ran from her vehicle and collapsed in the front yard of a nearby house. Thompkins cradled her while holding the knife to his own throat, Franklin said.
A witness attempted to help the victim, but Thompkins threatened them, pointing the knife at them and yelling for them to get back.
Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, Maryland State Police and Maryland Natural Resources Police, responded to the stabbing.
Franklin said Thompkins punctured his own neck with a knife while running to the woods to evade officers.
After 15 minutes and the use of multiple non-lethal methods, including a taser, a state trooper was able to knock the knife out of Thompkins' hand to detain him, police said.
Both Thompkins and the woman were flown to the University of Maryland Shock Trauma Center in Baltimore for treatment of their injuries.
After his arrest, a judge found Thompkins incompetent to stand trial in April 2022. He was committed to the Maryland Department of Health until August 2023, then transferred back to a local detention center upon being found competent, according to court filings.
Following his release, Thompkins will be placed on five years of supervised probation. He will also be required to complete mental health treatment.

title: Safe Chain Solutions to settle alleged counterfeit HIV drug claims
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Safe Chain Solutions to settle alleged counterfeit HIV drug claims

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 754
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Over two years of civil litigation against Cambridge-based pharmaceutical distributor Safe Chain Solutions relating to its alleged implication in a counterfeit HIV drug scheme has reached a settlement, according to federal court documents.A consent judgment and permanent injunction filed Feb. 20 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York is awaiting a signature from a federal judge, which will formally settle Gilead Sciences Inc's complex lawsuit against the local pharmaceutical distributor and its founders, brothers Charlie and Patrick Boyd.
Gilead is a biopharmaceutical company that develops and markets a variety of medications, including drugs that treat or prevent HIV.
The complaint, originally filed in 2021 and amended in 2022, alleged Safe Chain's involvement in the distribution of authentic-looking bottles of two of Gilead's HIV medications, Biktarvy and Descovy, to pharmacies across the country.
Gilead's deeper investigation into the alleged scheme revealed that some of the bottles contained completely different drugs not used to treat HIV. Some of the bottles reportedly contained quetiapine, or Seroquel XR — an antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder, according to the amended complaint.
The complaint alleged that some of the counterfeit bottles purchased from Safe Chain, which were received by pharmacies and later reported to the pharmacies by customers, came with falsified pedigrees, or documentation, that claimed to trace the drugs back to an authentic source.
The consent judgment and permanent injunction will prohibit Safe Chain from selling any Gilead product in the United States, including a number of Gilead's HIV medications.
Under the terms of the agreement, Gilead will have the right to have an independent firm audit Safe Chain's purchase and sales records for all products bought and sold after the consent judgment is entered, according to the document.
The firm will not provide information to Gilead unless it relates to Gilead-branded products or non-compliance with the order.
Additionally, Safe Chain will be required to relinquish its rights to over $2.7 million in frozen assets, which includes over $1.9 million of Safe Chain's funds in an equitable trust account and money in the brothers' personal investment and life insurance accounts.
If a court finds that Safe Chain violated any terms of the consent judgment and injunction, the company would be required to pay Gilead 100 times the wholesale acquisition cost of the Gilead product sold, according to the document.
The wholesale acquisition cost for Biktarvy is over $3,000. Descovy is over $2,000.
Despite the lawsuit's allegations, Safe Chain believes that the drugs "were actually legitimate Gilead products that had been diverted into the stream of commerce," said August Matteis, an attorney for the the company.
In counterclaims against Gilead, Safe Chain alleged that Gilead's accusations were "false and defamatory" and that Gilead was "motivated by trying to destroy the secondary market for its drugs," he said.
According to Matteis, Safe Chain believes Gilead sued the company in "an attempt to cover up the fact that thousands of bottles of Gilead HIV drugs entered the stream of commerce due to poor oversight of Gilead's free drug access program in Florida."
"There has been no judicial ruling on Gilead's claims against Safe Chain or on Safe Chain's counterclaims against Gilead," he said. "Safe Chain agreed to settle this case to end the legal costs associated with this litigation and to get back to running its business."
Gilead's lawsuit was not the only documentation explaining concerns with Safe Chain.
A June 2023 warning letter issued by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration detailed the company's violations of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act. It followed the FDA's monthlong inspection of Safe Chain's Cambridge facility from April to May 2022.
Specifically, it called the company out for not having adequate verification systems required under law that "may have resulted in suspect product entering the supply chain" rather than being quarantined, according to the letter.
The letter also confirmed that Safe Chain purchased products from other drug wholesalers that were not authorized, failed to maintain records of suspect product investigations and failed to respond to notifications of illegitimate products.
The Feb. 20 injunction prohibiting Safe Chain from selling Gilead products ensures that Safe Chain "will never again be a source of counterfeit versions of our medicines," according to a Gilead spokesperson.
"This is the latest result of years of work reflecting our longstanding commitment to protect patients and the public from bad actors selling counterfeit and illicit versions of Gilead's medicines," the spokesperson said in an email. "This includes working closely with the FDA, FBI and prosecutors to dismantle this counterfeiting network, deter bad actors, and thwart illegal pharmaceutical distribution."

title: There are other options open to poultry farmers
author: DR. ASHA SUBRAMANIAN
content:
There are other options open to poultry farmers

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DR. ASHA SUBRAMANIAN | Section: News 
 
 726
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As a physician, I have been following closely our country's bird flu crisis. I was saddened but not surprised to learn that, within days of each other, bird flu was detected for the first time on an Eastern Shore poultry farm and our country experienced the death of its first patient from H5N1 bird flu in Louisiana.My colleagues and I are watchful for symptoms of bird flu and are hopeful that Maryland does not join the list of states in which more than 60 human cases of bird flu have been detected. I applaud our public health officials for doing what they can to keep the bird flu from spreading but the reality is that the virus has sickened dozens of people, decimated poultry populations and infected dairy cows.
Thankfully, our state is doing a good job of monitoring for the virus. But now is the time to take a hard look at the food production system that puts farm workers in close contact with sick birds and cows, the Standard American Diet that demands it and the health ramifications of both.
From a doctor's perspective, shifting food production away from intensive animal agriculture can benefit public health. Facilities with large numbers of animals in a small amount of space are a concern for public health because they provide ideal conditions for viruses to spread, evolve and possibly acquire the ability to more easily infect people. Intensive animal agriculture was implicated when influenza viruses H1N1, H5N1 and N7N9 jumped from animals to people, according to research published in Frontiers in Microbiology.
The life of a contract chicken grower can be challenging, and some of them are repurposing their chicken houses to grow crops. I was not surprised to learn that North Carolina poultry farmers Dale and Paula Boles switched from chickens, converted their 500-foot-long poultry barn to a greenhouse and now grow organic vegetables. They are not alone. In Southwest Arkansas, farmers Jennifer and Rodney Barrett are transitioning from raising poultry and cattle to growing mushrooms.
These farm transitions aren't easy. The government should provide financial and technical support. Maryland could help its farmers with a program like the one established by lawmakers in Vermont who provide grants to farmers who wish to diversify or transition from one type of farming to another. On a broader scale, U.S. Sen. Cory Booker has introduced legislation that would require the U.S. Department of Agriculture to provide grants to livestock farmers to pay off related debt and to transition the property to alternative agriculture activities. Maryland's U.S. Sens. Van Hollen and Alsobrooks should support this legislation to help ensure that it passes.
According to the USDA, "Maryland is small, but it reaches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Appalachian Mountains, providing a suitable environment for a variety of agricultural commodities," which means lots of opportunities for farmers. Sweet corn, hazelnuts, watermelons, grapes, as well as apple, cherry and peach orchards are just a few promising options.
Shifting away from animal agriculture helps our environment and improves worker safety as well. Maryland's poultry farms are a primary source of water, air and land pollution. Improving the water quality in the Chesapeake Bay is another reason to increase acreage of fruit and nut trees. One way to keep phosphorous and other pollutants from flowing into rivers is to install riparian buffers of trees and shrubs to intercept polluted water running off of fields where chicken litter has been applied. Trees that are suitable for riparian buffers, like hazelnuts can also provide income to farmers.
I have found for myself and my patients that removing animal products from the diet improves health too. A plant-based diet focused on fruits, veggies, legumes and grains grown in Maryland can help maintain healthy weight, lower blood pressure and improve heart health.
I know this from my own personal experience and from treating patients with diet-related diseases, and the scientific literature tells the same story. A recent study with 22 pairs of identical twins found that a plant-based diet improves heart health in as little as eight weeks. The twins following a plant-based diet experienced lower LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, and they lost more weight than the omnivore twins.
Government grants and other assistance should also be available if Maryland poultry farmers or egg producers would like to switch to growing crops and planting orchards, which will also benefit human health and the environment.

title: Letter had no good reasoning
author: Staff Writer
content:
Letter had no good reasoning

 January 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 397
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Sometimes you publish letters to the editor that contain strong political views that are based on false information or bad logic or both.When a political view is based on good reasoning, I don't feel the need to respond. But I do feel the need to respond when a writer gets published with no good reasoning. Such is the case with Mr. Adrian's letter "Gone down a dark road," in Sunday's 14 January edition.
His letter is filled with false statements. For example, he claims that Democrats control elections to push some kind of agenda. There is no evidence for that. Quite the contrary. Mr. Adrian somehow completely missed the well-known information that Republicans are involved in managing elections. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of examples.
Even the head Republican, Donald Trump, knew that when he called the Republicans who control elections asking them to alter votes in 2020. As another example, Mr. Adrian seems to claim that harvesting crops in the fall leads to harvesting ballots. I don't think there is any evidence for that.
But what really gets me is the use of questions for arguments. This illogical method of argument is a tool of conspiracy theorists and despots for thousands of years. "When did you stop beating your spouse?" is the classic retort to that entire form of reasoning.
Mr. Adrian received a document about mail-in ballots and points out he could print it. "What could possibly go wrong?" he writes as if that question is a legitimate argument against the entire process. Without evidence, the question makes no sense, any more than me asking Mr. Adrian when he stopped beating people. Mr. Adrian should read about how the Arizona Republican Party spent millions of tax dollars on a month's-long audit of ballots that only showed Mr. Biden's votes were undercounted. Georgia audited their elections three times by hand counting ballots and found no fraud. These are just two facts out of hundreds of examples that belie the assumption underlying Mr. Adrian's question.
Mr. Adrian poses many other questions that assume evidence where none exists. And he ends his letter with the question, "Which political party controls the Board of Elections anyway?" as if that is a reason for everyone to doubt elections. It is not.
All available evidence is that elections in Maryland are fair and honest. People should appreciate that and take the time to vote.
MICHAEL DAVIS
Easton

title: ‘Hello Girl’ from Maryland may soon win a medal for her WWI service
author: ROBERT STEWART Capital News Service
content:
‘Hello Girl’ from Maryland may soon win a medal for her WWI service

 December 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ROBERT STEWART Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 955
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Marie Edmee LeRoux has been buried at the Fort Lincoln Cemetery here for 79 years, but she may soon win a gold medal for her service in World War I.LeRoux was one of 223 bilingual women deployed to France as telephone operators, often under combat conditions, as part of the U.S. Army Signal Corps. They were the country's first women soldiers, popularly known as the "Hello Girls."
They've been long overlooked for their service. But now the U.S. Congress has approved a special congressional gold medal as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for the coming year. The measure now goes to President Joe Biden for consideration.
"It's a story that's been forgotten and needs to be told," LeRoux's granddaughter, Catherine Bourgin of McLean, Va., said. "With the passage of the Congressional gold medal, that's what I want."
Women like LeRoux braved German submarines on the transport to the war front and disease and bombardment to serve in the signal corps under the American Expeditionary Forces. Their service helped set a precedent for women's service in the U.S. military and influenced support for the 19th amendment, guaranteeing women the right to vote.
Gen. John Pershing requested that bilingual women operators deploy to France. They were more skilled and experienced at operating the new telephone systems of the time, and the AEF needed bilingual people to communicate with the French forces.
LeRoux had those skills. She was born in Montreal and grew up speaking French and English before moving to the U.S. at age 10, according to Bourgin. She was a passionate singer but, according to Bourgin, LeRoux abandoned her music career to answer the call.
LeRoux traveled to France in 1918, operating the switchboards that connected military commanders with the front lines and their French counterparts. She stayed in France after the war to restart her music studies. When war threatened France again in 1939, LeRoux fled the country with her 4-year-old daughter in tow. She eventually came to live near family in Prince George's County.
She passed away in 1945 and was interred in an unmarked grave here, according to her granddaughter. She did not receive a military headstone because she was not considered a veteran.
Many women who served in the U.S. Army signal corps found out they weren't considered "soldiers" when they applied for benefits after the war. They received no veteran medical care and no federally funded rehabilitation training.
This was only remedied in 1977 when Congress acknowledged them as veterans, following decades of petitioning by Hello Girls like Merle Egan Anderson. Most had already passed away by then.
While Bourgin was researching her grandmother's history, she discovered LeRoux was a member of the Hello Girls. She also learned that a congressional commission had recommended these female veterans receive a Congressional Gold Medal collectively.
So, in 2023, Bourgin began working with others to help her grandmother and the other Hello Girls get that medal.
Bourgin refers to the advocacy group as the "Hello Girls Family," and she joined them to bring their story to Capitol Hill. Elizabeth Cobbs' 2017 book also helped reintroduce the women operators' war contribution into the mainstream.
"The telephone," Cobbs said, "was the only way that they could rapidly communicate with troops who were facing mechanized onslaughts of the most destructive machinery ever devised by humans."
Women could operate the war switchboards faster than their male counterparts, she said. They couldn't even vote at the time, nor serve on juries in most states.
Chris Christopher led the advocacy charge.
As a former staffer on the World War I Centennial Commission that recommended in 2018 that the Hello Girls receive the award as part of the country's formal efforts to commemorate the war, Christopher thought getting the award across the finish line was important. In 2023, with no bill passed, Christopher decided to tackle the issue head-on.
"I sat down," Christopher said, "and wrote a letter to every single senator who was not already a co-sponsor."
If a senator was not a co-sponsor, Christopher said, he researched and included World War I registration documents of a relative or ancestor of that senator to personalize the letters. He then made sure those were hand-delivered to the senators.
Volunteering in his free time, he also coordinated the network of history buffs and Hello Girl descendants and supporters for virtual meetings and lobbying on the Hill.
Catherine Bourgin had just discovered her grandmother's unmarked grave in Fort Lincoln Cemetery, in a plot next to her great-grandmother's. She also connected with Christopher at the same time.
Bourgin said her grandmother's grave was symbolic of what happened to the Hello Girls. LeRoux was in an unmarked grave, Bourgin said, just miles from the nation's capital but nevertheless lost to history.
While lobbying on Capitol Hill a few months later, Bourgin said, she told other advocates about the unmarked grave. The group got fired up, she said, and decided to change that.
They procured the grave marker and arranged for a military honors ceremony at the cemetery.
"The folks that did what they did for my grandmother," Bourgin said, "they truly made an indelible mark on my family's history."
Bourgin thinks the ceremony drew attention to the gold-medal cause. They made sure members of Congress were invited.
Now it seems the advocacy may have worked. Senators are expected to take up the defense act in the coming days.
Both Bourgin and Christopher hope that the award will bring attention to the untold stories of the country's first female soldiers, and ensure that all of them have veteran's grave markers.
"There are so many stories out there like this," Bourgin said, "and we just have to discover them."
"Hopefully once we get past all this, this is going to be something that will generate an ongoing effort," Christopher said. He wants "to get all of the Hello Girls their appropriate grave marker."

 A 17-year-old boy is recovering after being shot during an unsanctioned car meet in an industrial park near Newark.The incident happened just before 1:30 a.m. Sunday on Tyler Way in the Delaware Industrial Park, located off South Chapel Street between Scottfield and Interstate 95.

title: Caps fill void, acquire Thompson
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Caps fill void, acquire Thompson

 June 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 751
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Tampa Bay Lightning and Washington Capitals were active Saturday during rounds 2-7 of the NHL draft, each making multiple moves to shake up their rosters for next season and beyond.Tampa Bay sent two-time Stanley Cup-winning defenseman Mikhail Sergachev to Utah and depth forward Tanner Jeannot to Los Angeles in moves that cleared more than $11 million in salary cap space. That could be enough money to keep captain and face of the franchise Steven Stamkos or make a significant free agent signing, and it will go a long way to providing room to lock up cornerstone defenseman Victor Hedman with a long-term contract extension.
The Lightning got younger on the blue line by receiving 24-year-old defenseman J.J. Moser, along with forward prospect Conor Geekie and two draft picks for Sergachev, who was signed through 2031 making $8.5 million annually. A 2025 second-rounder and a fourth this year allows Tampa Bay to restock its prospect pool after making eight consecutive playoff appearances, winning two titles and reaching the final three times.
That contending window remains wide open, and general manage Julien BriseBois now has flexibility to retool on the fly with free agency opening Monday. Stamkos staying is a possibility, and now the Lightning have the opportunity to pursue one or more of the top wingers available, a group that includes Jake Guentzel, Patrick Kane and Jonathan Marchessault.
The Capitals already did their big-name hunting last week by acquiring highly paid center Pierre-Luc Dubois from the Kings for goaltender Darcy Kuemper. On Saturday, they filled that void in net by acquiring Logan Thompson from host Vegas for a pair of third-round picks.
Thompson figures to split time with Charlie Lindgren in a tandem costing less than $2 million total next season, with a year left on each goalie's contract. Thompson, 27, was an All-Star and played 37 games for the Golden Knights during their 2022-23 championship run before getting injured before the playoffs.
"I got a lot more that I can prove in this league and I'm hoping that I get that opportunity with Washington," said Thompson, who was in bed when he was informed of the trade and hurried to the Sphere for a previously scheduled autograph signing. "Actually, it was a good alarm clock. I woke up to that and then obviously get ready and come down, and I knew it was going to be an interesting day."
Long before getting his name engraved on the Stanley Cup, Thompson got his first foray into the NHL Capitals development camp in the summer of 2018. He played for Washington at back-to-back prospect showcases, went to training camp with the American Hockey League's Hershey Bears in 2019, starred for the ECHL's South Carolina and earned his first contract as a result.
"I'm thankful for the Washington goalie department every day," Thompson told The Associated Press at 2023 All-Star Weekend. "They're the reason why I'm here. They're the only team that gave me a chance three years ago. If it wasn't for them, I wouldn't be here today."
Washington also traded fourth-line winger Beck Malenstyn to Buffalo for the 43rd pick, taking U.S.-born defenseman Cole Hutson, and traded up in the third round to select Ilya Protas, the younger brother of Capitals forward Aliaksei Protas. Malenstyn, 26, is a restricted free agent with arbitration rights who had 21 points in 81 games during his first full NHL season and gives the Sabres Buffalo valuable forward depth as they try to end the league's longest playoff drought.
Looking to end the longest Stanley Cup drought, the Toronto Maple Leafs took a step toward upgrading their defense by acquiring the rights to pending free agent Chris Tanev from Dallas for a 2026 seventh-round pick. The trade gives Toronto the first crack at signing the valuable 24-year-old top-four defenseman.
Vegas moved quickly to replenish goalie depth by acquiring Akira Schmid from New Jersey along with young forward Alexander Holtz in a trade that sent Paul Cotter and a third-rounder to the Devils. Among the other moves, St. Louis traded Kevin Hayes and a '25 second-rounder to Pittsburgh for future considerations to shed the remainder of the his contract, and Boston sent Jakob Lauko to Minnesota for Vinni Lettieri in a swap of centers that also involved draft picks.
The Sabres after getting Malenstyn began the process of buying out the contract of forward Jeff Skinner, GM Kevyn Adams confirmed at the conclusion of the draft. The buyout saves Buffalo $7.5 million next season while spreading out money owed to Skinner against the cap through 2030.
