White House OKs Maryland wind energy project

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KATHARINE WILSON Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 959
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — Offshore wind energy is coming to Maryland, and with it, union jobs.The Biden administration on Thursday approved Baltimore-based US Wind's project to build offshore wind turbines about 10 miles off the coast of Ocean City, Maryland.
The offshore wind farm could generate over two gigawatts of wind energy and power over 718,000 homes, according to the Department of the Interior.
President Joe Biden said in a statement that the wind energy industry had been "struggling to gain a foothold" in the years before he came into office.
"From manufacturing and shipbuilding to port operations and construction, this industry will support tens of thousands of good-paying and union jobs, provide reliable clean power to homes and businesses, strengthen our power grid against outages, and help reduce pollution — all while protecting biodiversity and marine ecosystems," the president said.
Maryland Energy Administration Director Paul Pinsky called the Biden administration's action "an important step forward in the effort to bring clean, renewable energy production to Maryland's coast."
"Today's announcement underscores the careful, comprehensive and collaborative environmental analysis that has gone into these projects," Pinsky said in a statement.
The Maryland project is the tenth commercial-scale offshore wind energy project approved by the Biden administration. Combined, the projects are projected to generate 15 gigawatts of clean energy, half of Biden's goal of 30 gigawatts of offshore wind-produced energy by 2030.
The Maryland project includes up to 114 wind turbines, four offshore substation platforms and a meteorological tower. There will be three phases to the US Wind project, two of which — called MarWin and Momentum Wind — have already received offshore renewable energy certificates from the state.
Energy is set to start flowing in December 2028 from the first phase of the project. The final project is expected to be completed in late 2027 or early 2028, according to the plan submitted by US Wind.
The approval is a win for Maryland environmental groups and the state government, which have been working for offshore wind power in the state for around 10 years.
Starting in 2013, the Maryland legislature passed a series of bills to set offshore wind energy projects in motion.
The state set a goal in 2023, through the Promoting Offshore Wind Energy Resources Act, to generate 8.5 gigawatts of power from offshore wind by 2031.
This goal has hit some road bumps along the way, including the withdrawal of Denmark-based Ørsted's planned offshore wind projects in January.
US Wind won the competitive lease sale of the 46,970 acres of federal ocean waters in 2014.
"By moving away from reliance on dirty fossil fuel energy and building renewable energy, Marylanders will be able to breathe cleaner air and benefit from new clean energy jobs," Maryland Sierra Club Chapter Director Josh Tulkin said in a statement Thursday.
Jamie DeMarco, the federal campaigns coordinator for the Chesapeake Climate Action Network, said in an interview with Capital News Service that the Maryland wind farm is a milestone in moving offshore energy generation forward in Maryland.
"This is a huge undertaking to build an entire machine to deploy offshore wind, but once that machine is built, it'll be able to hum and crank out new domestic energy, and clean energy that's going to help us clean the air and meet our climate goals," DeMarco said.
Offshore wind turbines have been coming online across the East Coast, DeMarco said, but this will be the first operational offshore wind facility in Maryland.
Environmental advocates aren't the only celebrating parties. Union officials are touting the jobs set to be created by the wind farm.
Almost 2,680 jobs annually over seven years could be created during the development and construction phase of the wind farm, according to the Interior Department.
US Wind's planned permanent offshore wind components production facility, called Sparrows Point Steel in Sparrows Point, Baltimore — the former home of Bethlehem Steel — is forecast to generate jobs for steelworkers.
The Baltimore Bethlehem Steel mill, which closed in 2012, was once the largest steel producer in the world. Sparrows Point Steel will bring steelworker jobs back to Maryland, DeMarco said, in a way that hasn't been seen since the closure of Bethlehem.
Jim Strong, the offshore wind sector assistant for the United Steelworkers International Union, told CNS Thursday that the facility is expected to bring in over 500 jobs. The project will help not only steelworkers, Strong said, but other union trades as well.
"It's about addressing our climate crisis, about creating new green energy jobs — these will be high paid union jobs," Strong said.
Strong has served as a liaison between the union and US Wind. He said that the Sparrows Point facility has the opportunity to become a "central hub" for monopile production on the Atlantic Ocean. Monopiles, steel cylinders, are used for wind turbines, bridges and other projects, he said.
US Wind is a subsidiary of Italian company Renexia SpA.
The project has some detractors, like Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland), who represents the Eastern Shore.
"Offshore wind industrialization comes at a heavy cost to our marine life and environment, and is an incredibly expensive way to generate electricity," Harris said on X in July. "We should never allow foreign owned companies to control our energy supply — much less harm our environment while doing it."
The federal Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's director, Elizabeth Klein, said in a statement that the Maryland project "reflects the best available science and invaluable insights from Tribes, government agencies, local communities, industry leaders, ocean users, and environmental groups gathered during our extensive environmental review process."
"As we continue to support the undeniable momentum we see along our coasts, our focus remains on fostering responsible energy development, while protecting marine life and ecosystems," she said.
Democrats in the state, including Gov. Wes Moore, have been supportive of the project. Moore signed a memorandum of understanding with the federal government in June supporting offshore wind production.

title: The Oxford Museum celebrates 60 years with '60s theme
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
The Oxford Museum celebrates 60 years with '60s theme

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 537
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Wanda Whedbee knows her father would have been so proud to witness The Oxford Museum's 60th birthday party on Saturday.Whedbee's father, Lee Willey founded the museum in 1964. Whedbee said that six years later, Willey died of a heart attack, and so he didn't get to see the museum's growth over the years.
"I think it's amazing how it's grown," she said. "And the reason it has grown like this is because of the people that moved (into) town. And so many of them have taken an interest in it and worked so hard to keep it going."
For many years, Whedbee was a docent at the museum. When people would come in, she said she would point to the museum's first pieces — glassware and pottery that her father excavated from the grounds of the old Maryland Military and Naval Academy in town — and tell them about the museum's humble beginnings.
"And I would say, 'Look around. And if you really work hard, that's what you can accomplish,'" she said.
Saturday afternoon, community members had the opportunity to celebrate that growth — and another year around the sun for the museum — with the museum's current exhibit, "Oxford 1964: The Times They Were A-Changin,'" and cake and ice cream.
Terrie and Barry Smale, who haven't been to the museum in a decade, were blown away when they returned Saturday. They said it has transformed since their last visit.
Terrie's favorite part of the current exhibit was the 1960s area in the back corner of the museum, which was complete with vinyl records, a TV from the '60s and a rotary dial phone hanging on the wall. Terrie said she remembered having the same TV when she was growing up.
At the event, LIza Ledford and John Tochko were named winners of the Doug Hanks Jr. Oxford Preservation Award, which recognizes the efforts of people or organizations to preserve Oxford's history and heritage.
Ledford, who is the executive director of the Oxford Community Center, said the award means everything to her.
"It means the world to me to feel recognized by the public and the town, and just to feel that people are appreciating the stuff we're putting out there," she said.
Ledford has been with the community center for seven years. She said she feels lucky that what she loves to do every day is getting appreciated by the community.
"Thank you to everyone who was part of making this happen," she said. "And I share it with everybody who's part of the Oxford Community Center."
Tochko, who could not be in attendance Saturday, has been chairman of the Museum Building Committee for the last few years. When the winners were announced, Tochko was praised for his "quiet" support of different local organizations over the years and his involvement with the community center.
Because of the high temperatures outside, the museum's birthday party was held inside the museum Saturday afternoon. The Oxford Museum Executive Director Julie Wells said she knew the event would be crowded if it was held inside the museum.
"But we like being with each other," she said, later adding, "This is such a happy event."
The Oxford Museum is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Fridays through Mondays. Admission is free.

title: Julia Child's kitchen at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Julia Child's kitchen at the library

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Monday, March 3, at 6 p.m., in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, it will be my honor to interview Paula Johnson about her newest book, "Julia Child's Kitchen: The Design, Tools, Stories, and Legacy of an Iconic Space."Full disclosure: Johnson is a lifelong friend of mine. She is also a distinguished curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Among her many curatorial triumphs, it was Johnson and co-curator Rayna Green that brought Julia Child's kitchen to the museum in 2001. Almost a quarter of a century later, it remains one of that institution's most popular exhibits.
I was one of the lucky fellows who received a copy of Johnson's new book when it came out in October.
Initially, truth be told, I wasn't sure what I would think of a book about a kitchen, fool that I am. Anyone who knows Julia Child, read her books or watched her television shows, knows that a book about Julia Child's kitchen is a book about Julia Child.
It's been a long time since I've had so much fun reading a book.
And the word "fun" is apt. Again and again in the book, as people recall cooking with Child in her kitchen or a meal they shared there, the word they use to describe both their host and the place is "fun."
Which is not to say that serious labor did not take place in that kitchen.
The book makes it clear that Child and her husband Paul were both workhorses. In the early television shows, the sponsoring public television station, WGBH Boston, couldn't afford retakes or editing. Julia had to begin upon a complicated recipe, carry it through, instructing all along, and arrive at a finished product that she could take a bite out of in just 28 minutes flat. The cameras shut off at 28 minutes, and there was no going back.
To accomplish this feat of legerdemain, she and Paul would practice for hours at home before a show, choosing which elements of a recipe to demonstrate, deciding how to demonstrate those elements and carefully working out the language to use in explaining them.
The whole thing was choreographed from beginning to end and different stages of the cooking prepared in advance so that, "through the magic of TV," they could be displayed at the proper time as if just pulled from the oven.
Yet somehow, Julia always came across as relaxed and enjoying herself. And it wasn't a guise.
One of the things I found most endearing about "Julia Child's Kitchen" is the way sections on subjects such as the kitchen's organizing principles inevitably end up revealing the love Paul Child felt for his wife, the care he took in setting up that kitchen and showcasing her art. In letters to his brother, Paul sometimes referred to his wife as "Julie."
Julia called her kitchen "the soul of the house," and her nephew, Alex Prud'homme, called the table where meals were served in that kitchen "the center of the universe."
Unsurprisingly for that time and a family of their class, the Childs had a formal dining room, but Julia's preferred place to serve friends a meal was the kitchen. Julia's unpretentious attitude toward entertaining (and herself) is made clear in her explanation for the placement of that kitchen table, "I want the dining table in the middle of the room because, like a sheepdog, I need to be right there in the midst of everyone."
That statement is so characteristic of the woman we meet in Johnson's book. Julia Child never fails to charm, yet somehow she never seems to patronize or fawn.
The book itself is like a party at Julia's house. You meet fascinating people, hear terrific stories, experience a magical place, and, at the very least, get to imagine yourself enjoying extraordinary meals.
Speaking of stories, I can tell you from long experience that the author of "Julia Child's Kitchen" is a great storyteller in person as well as in her writing. And so I ask the pleasure of your company on March 3 at 6 p.m. for an evening in Julia Child's kitchen, courtesy of the Smithsonian's Paula Johnson. Trust me, you're in for a real treat.

title: Talbot school board sees test scores, improvement initiatives
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot school board sees test scores, improvement initiatives

 September 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 836
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — State test scores released last month show a slight increase in math and English proficiency levels at both the district and state levels.Talbot County's Board of Education discussed that trend and others during a work session on Monday, taking a first deep dive into the test results from 2023-2024's Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program.
In English, 47.3% of Talbot County Public Schools students tested proficient, a jump of 2.8% from 44.5% in 2022-2023. In math, 18.3% of students were proficient, up 1.1% from 17.2% the year prior. The district slots in 14th and 18th, respectively, in those categories among the state's 24 districts.
ENGLISH TRENDS"One of the things that the board is always interested in is how does Talbot County Public Schools compare to other districts in the state," said Helga Einhorn, assistant superintendent of school leadership, while presenting the English results. "And I wish that I could give you better news and say that we have flip-flopped the map, but if you compare this year's results to last year across the state, you will see very little change. There is not a single district in the state who is leapfrogging in improvements on this map."
Einhorn and Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi emphasized that the district internally tracks student learning levels. This is done at benchmarks throughout the year.
"I can assure this board that more than 47% of our students are mastering grade level standards," Einhorn said of the English proficiency rate. "It's just that they are not showing it across the state on this particular assessment."
Some positives for the English rates included third grade proficiency and the growth for certain cohorts and subgroups. Third grade English proficiency saw a significant jump from the 2022-2023 school year.
Einhorn pointed out that in 2023, sixth grade students were 40.1% proficient. That same group of students came in at 43.8% proficient on the seventh grade test. "For that cohort of students, it's growth," Einhorn said.
Einhorn said all student groups saw growth in English rates, though Black students had the smallest increase.
"We are reaching every student in some sense, in some capacity," Board President Emily Jackson said of the subgroups. "Maybe not as well as we could, but we're getting there, we are making growth, and that's what I want to see."
MATH TRENDSIn math, the district has many initiatives to increase proficiency. Einhorn said the number of elementary math coaches has increased from three to six, along with an addition of one middle school math coach.
The district is implementing an adaptive testing program called Measures of Academic Progress for kindergarten through eighth grade to track student growth.
In 2023-2024's state test scores, TCPS students showed increases across the board.
"We see slight increases for each one of our student groups," Einhorn said. "We have less of an increase for our Hispanic and Latino students. And we still continue to have fewer than 5% of our Black students and our multilingual learners proficient in mathematics."
For proficiency levels below 5%, the state does not indicate exact percentages. Of the 24 districts, the Talbot district is one of three below the 5% mark in math proficiency among Black students, and one of nine districts below the 5% mark in math proficiency among multilingual students.
Einhorn and Jackson each thanked the Talbot County Council for its commitment in funding education, particularly the math coaches in elementary schools.
"When you see movement like we did in third grade," Jackson said, "I think that we are making really intentional, really important, really good funding decisions that have a big impact on learning."
EXPERT REVIEWSAs required by the state's education initiative, Blueprint for Maryland's Future, experts vetted by the Maryland Department of Education will be reviewing school districts across the state. Einhorn said state reviewers will be visiting three elementary schools in Talbot County this year.
Those schools will be Chapel District Elementary, St. Michaels Elementary and White Marsh Elementary. They were chosen for separate reasons. Einhorn stated: Chapel for reviewers to look at literacy instruction, St. Michaels to review practices for multilingual learners and White Marsh due to success in state testing.
"They had significant growth in their math achievement across all grades in this last MCAP assessment," Einhorn said of White Marsh Elementary. "So they want to know what White Marsh is doing well."
Jackson asked how the district can take lessons learned from these three schools to its largest elementary school, Easton Elementary.
"Can you speak to how we plan to address that?" Jackson asked. "How do you take what you've learned at a very small, very specific population and duplicate it or replicate it at a school like Easton Elementary?"
"One of the things that we do even though it's a larger school, we have committed the same types of resources but just on a larger scale," Einhorn said. "So while our smaller elementaries might have one math coach, we see multiple math coaches to be able to service the number of classrooms that we have at Easton Elementary."
Einhorn said other schools in the district will have state reviews in the next year or two.

Marriott awards top honor to Easton Fairfield Inn

 EASTON — The Easton Fairfield Inn & Suites has been recognized as the 2023 Hotel of the Year by Marriott out of more than 1,000 Fairfield hotels worldwide.Tucked next to Chipotle off of U.S. Route 50 and Chapel Road, the hotel is managed by Hill Hospitality, a hotel development and management company. Chad Hill, the company's vice president, said the 82-room hotel stands out in more ways than one.
"This is not a prototypical Fairfield hotel," Hill said. He emphasized its cleanliness, customer service and customized designs that give the hotel a small-town, Eastern Shore feel.
Every year, Hill said Marriott checks into each hotel for a random inspection. Marriott assesses each hotel based on a set of standards, while separately soliciting feedback from recent guests. Based on these evaluations and guest review scores, a small percentage of hotels receive the Diamond Award, a recognition from Marriott of the highest performing tier of Fairfield hotels.
Of the 1,118 hotels evaluated, the Easton Fairfield Inn & Suites was rated fourth in intent to recommend, fifth in staff service and seventh in cleanliness.
The Easton Fairfield was recognized with the 2023 Diamond Award, marking its second consecutive year and third since opening in 2015. However, this year, the hotel went a step further when Marriott recognized it as Hotel of the Year within the Fairfield brand.
According to Cristina Shockley, Hill Hospitality's director of operations, the Easton hotel is a popular destination for corporate stays and those in town for weddings.
Shockley added that many of the employees are familiar with the Eastern Shore and its history and charm, a benefit for guests that are visiting for the first time. Some team members have been at the hotel since it opened, she said.
"We're so fortunate to have an incredible team," Hill said of the team that hovers around 23 employees.
Since the hospitality group is based in Easton, Hill said it's special to have the hometown property recognized at such a high level. Hill Hospitality manages six hotels, two each in Maryland and South Carolina, and one each in Maine and New York. Two additional hotels are in the works, including one in Fruitland that will open in June 2025.
"Every guest is given the opportunity to enjoy the charming small-town atmosphere that the Easton team provides when staying at our hotel," Shockley said in a written statement. "The Hotel of the Year award is a testament to the team's unwavering commitment to give the ultimate in guest service. title: Cambridge woman pleads guilty to altering evidence in Sidetracked Saloon shooting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge woman pleads guilty to altering evidence in Sidetracked Saloon shooting

 May 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Cambridge woman was handed a three-year sentence after pleading guilty to altering physical evidence in the shooting death of 23-year-old Antonio Smith.Judge Broughton Earnest handed down the sentence following a plea hearing on May 22. Chadnee Harris, 33, will serve 236 days followed by one year of probation, with the remainder of the sentence suspended.
Harris originally faced charges of of acting as an accessory after the fact of first- and second-degree murder and acting as an accessory after a felony for the same incident. The charges were amended to one count of altering physical evidence.
The charge stems from a shooting in the parking lot of Sidetracked Saloon in Easton on Sept. 30. Officers who responded to the incident just before 2 a.m. found Smith in the parking lot suffering from a gunshot wound to the head. Smith was transported to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton, where he was pronounced dead.
On May 20, Kevron Chase, 35, of Cambridge, pled guilty to first-degree murder for Smith's death. A sentencing hearing for Chase is set for July 19.
According to previous Star Democrat reporting, in charging documents, police said the bar's security camera footage showed Chase and Harris standing between two cars near the entrance of the bar and Smith approaching the two.
According to the documents, Chase pulled a handgun from his waistband area and pointed it at Smith. Chase put the handgun back toward his waistband area and then appeared to hand the gun to Harris, police said.
After a fight broke out, Harris reportedly walked toward the men. A crowd that had gathered quickly dispersed. According to the charging documents, Smith appeared to duck behind a car and Chase walked toward Smith, pointing a handgun at him. The officer who reviewed the footage wrote in charging documents that they saw a muzzle flash from the gun and Smith collapse in between two cars.
At Chase's plea hearing on May 20, Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale said Chase then left the scene and drove to Cambridge, where he disposed of the handgun in the Choptank River.
Chase and Harris were later found during a traffic stop on Race Street in Cambridge. They were both detained by police.

title: Evergreen Fresh - Cawley Tree Farm offers variety of fresh trees, greens
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Evergreen Fresh - Cawley Tree Farm offers variety of fresh trees, greens

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 15 | Section: News 
 
 773
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - They've been farming west of Denton more than 100 years, and for over a quarter of that century, Cawley Family Farm has branched out to become the only Christmas tree farm in Caroline County.On the Saturday after Thanksgiving, a steady stream of families rolled up the lane of the farm, past the festively decorated John Deere combine, past the Cawley family home and past a huge pavilion housing cut evergreen trees from North Carolina."It's a beautiful day," said owner Charles Cawley." It's going good. We've got good trees. I got some beautiful trees - a little pricier than last year but still beautiful trees - got a lot on the lot, as you can see. The Canaans are going out of here like crazy." In addition to Canaan firs, Cawley grows Concolor and Douglas firs, blue spruce and white pine - all on about 15 acres of the farm."We can't grow Frasers, so we bring them in," Cawley said."But we're the only one that brings in a tree, recuts it and puts it in holding tanks. No one else does that. So we sell the freshest pre-cut trees you can buy." "They're very hard to get, but we've got some beautiful Frasers," he said.Cawley said it took him a while, but he "got to how to grow" Canaan firs about 15 years ago.He pampers them, irrigating, spoon-feeding and growing them in "real thick grass. It helps keep the roots cooler because it gets too hot here," he said.According to the National Christmas Tree Association, the Canaan fir is a "relative newcomer to the Christmas tree market, with many similarities to both Fraser and balsam firs." About 500 to 600 trees are brought in from North Carolina."We sold about 200 off the lot, so we're selling between 700 and 800 a year," Cawley said.Keeping the trees fresh is important to Cawley. "When we sell one of these (Frasers) they'll hold the needles as long as one of those out in the field," he said. "And these things drink a lot of water initially. I mean, we just got these the day before Thanksgiving, and I had to fill these tanks up a couple times, they soaked up that much water." Once the trees are rehydrated, they are shaken, drilled with a tapered bit, set up on a pin stand in a shallow steel basin and kept watered. The operation has two drilling machines, three shakers and plenty of water holding bins inside and outdoors.The 55-foot by 80-foot pavilion can be closed off when the wind whips up to keep the trees from dehydrating. "If we had to add a little heat, we can, but we haven't had to," he said.Cawley clearly takes pride in his product, and his family pitches in. Arriving at 7 a.m. was his 7-year-old grandson Bryant, ready to get started - and put in a 12-hour day.Cawley's eldest daughter, Amy, makes wreaths and wood-burned ornaments from slices of sawed off stumps. The focus is on customer service, so other family members, as well as employees, wait on customers, shake needles from trees, wrap net around them and tote them to cars.Cawley is vice president of the Maryland Christmas Tree Association. He said he started out as a farmer, "but I did a lot of things in the meantime," even working for "all three levels of government - county, state and federal. You don't build this by just farming. It takes something else," Cawley said, adding that his wife Jane is a retired school nurse.Several years of drought, along with root aphids in the Douglass firs and scale on some Canaans, have affected the growth and aesthetics of a few trees in the field, so Cawley has to be vigilant."There's a challenge every year," he said.Cawley Family Farm Christmas tree sales began Nov. 21.You can visit 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.Friday, Saturday and Sunday, and on Monday to Thursday by appointment. The farm is located at 24320 Willow Pond Road, Denton. For more information, call 410-479-4780 or 410-829-4781, or email info@cawley.farm. The website is www.cawleyfarms.com.

Charles Cawley of Cawley Family Farm takes pride in the freshness of his cut Fraser firs from North Carolina.
 
CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Bryant Cawley enjoys helping out as he carries cut evergreen branches to the wreath-making greenhouse.
 
CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Amy Cawley of Cawley Family Farm in Denton creates a variety of wood-burned Christmas ornaments from the trunks of cut evergreen trees.
 
CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Charles Cawley demonstrates how cut trees from North Carolina are rehydrated before they are ready to be sold.
 
CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT

title: Local student wins national essay contest
author: DERECK SARIER Special to the Bay Times Record Observer / Star Democrat
content:
Local student wins national essay contest

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DERECK SARIER Special to the Bay Times Record Observer / Star Democrat | Section: Entertainment 
 
 443
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Viana Johnston, an eighth grade student attending Lighthouse Christian Academy in Stevensville, has been recently recognized as the national middle school winner of a Bill of Rights Essay contest hosted by the Stanley M. Herzog Foundation.The Herzog Foundation is a national organization dedicated to "advancing Christian education." The foundation enriches Christian (K-12) education by creating and leading various programs.
One of these programs was the 2023 Bill of Rights Essay Contest. All middle and high school students enrolled in a Christian school or those homeschooled in the U.S. were eligible to participate. Winners were selected from one middle school and one high school. Each winner would go on to receive $250 from the Herzog Foundation. The winners' schools also received an additional $250.
Participants were asked to answer these questions in three pages or less, "What made the Bill of Rights so revolutionary and unique when it was ratified? How has the Bill of Rights shaped our country?"
In an excerpt from Viana's eloquently crafted three-page essay, the middle school winner wrote, "The Bill of Rights is famous for that little, life-changing word: freedom, but what most people don't realize is that these documents weren't written overnight. Real people struggled, wrestled, and mulled over each word and phrase that went into the Bill of Rights, until it was finally ratified on December 15, 1791. Not only was it composed through much time and consideration but it secured the rights of people today granting our blessed country to grow, expand, and enter new times of innovation. It summarized what we stood for then and stand for now. It lets a person breathe, work, and earn their way to success."
The Herzog Foundation announced Viana, daughter of George and Cathy Johnston, as the middle school winner of the contest in December. Johnston received the prize money and a trophy for her achievement.
In a release announcing the winners, Herzog Foundation Chairman Todd Graves said, "The Bill of Rights was ratified over 230 years ago and still stands as a beacon for our most fundamental rights as Americans. It's crucial that all young students understand the significance of this founding document."
Kathy Guerra, head of Lighthouse Christian Academy, stated the school was initially in disbelief, as this was the first time their school had made an entry to a contest of this magnitude. However, they were not surprised that Viana had won, as she is a gifted writer who creates masterworks of art with her words. "Viana is an inquisitive, energetic, and ambitious student," says Guerra, who "seeks to excel in all of her subjects."
To learn more about the Herzog Foundation and the programs it has to offer, visit www.herzog foundation.com.

title: CWDI responds to Cambridge commissioners' lawsuit
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI responds to Cambridge commissioners' lawsuit

 May 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 865
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Executive Director Matt Leonard sees the lawsuit filed earlier this month against CWDI by the Commissioners of Cambridge as a threat to the progress of the Cambridge Harbor project."We had no choice but to respond," Leonard said in a press release May 14. "The city's lawsuit has its facts wrong and threatens the significant progress CWDI is making on behalf of the community to finally realize the 30-year vision for Cambridge's waterfront."
On May 14, CWDI and CWDI Holdings filed a response to the lawsuit filed against them and Yacht Maintenance Company in Dorchester County Circuit Court on May 1.
The lawsuit, which was amended May 3, alleges CWDI is in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. It seeks $75,000 in damages and requests temporary, preliminary and permanent injunctions stopping defendants from transferring any portion of the property in violation of the covenants of the 2021 transfer agreement.
According to court documents, CWDI's May 14 response to the suit argues that the city's complaint "is the product of the well-publicized frustrations of the recently departed city manager," Tom Carroll. The response alleges Carroll has "sought to undermine CWDI" for the past eight months.
CWDI's response replies to the commissioners' claims about the property transfer agreement and the right of CWDI Holdings to be in possession of the property.
In the lawsuit filed May 1, the commissioners mention Section 6E of the transfer agreement, which states, "no portion of the property may be transferred unless the proposed use of the subject parcel(s) is 'shovel ready' (with permits, financing and groundbreaking within 90-days of closing)..."
The May 1 suit also mentions Exhibit C of the agreement that "CWDI will not transfer, subdivide or encumber all or any portion of the property" until reaching a definitive agreement with a developer or developers. That developer must come from a developer request for proposal process, which is outlined in the transfer agreement.
The commissioners argue in the May 1 lawsuit that CWDI violated this in March 2022 by transferring city-donated property to CWDI Holdings, a limited liability company.
CWDI states in its response that the city and CWDI agreed to CWDI creating CWDI Holdings to hold title to property named in the property transfer agreement. CWDI also states this was agreed to in a 2022 amendment to a 2014 state transfer agreement.
In response to city allegations that CWDI has not gone through the request for proposal process to choose a developer, CWDI alleges in court documents that Exhibit C of the transfer agreement gives leeway to seek a master developer or combination of individual project developers for all or parts of the Cambridge Harbor project. CWDI states it issued a request for proposals, called "Request for Expressions of Interest for Redevelopment," on July 15 and issued a press release Nov. 22 summarizing proposals it had received.
In its response, CWDI discusses its plans to sell a piece of property from the 2021 transfer agreement to Yacht Maintenance. In the court document, CWDI states that it has been transparent with its intentions regarding Yacht Maintenance. It says CWDI would "routinely" update the city on the status of negotiations to convey the property to Yacht Maintenance.
CWDI's response states that the lot line revision needed for the sale of the property had been finalized and executed by both parties and delivered to Cambridge's Planning and Zoning Department on April 29.
"CWDI cannot conceive of any legitimate explanation why, more than two weeks later, the document has not yet been signed and recorded," the court document says.
The press release — sent out the same day as the response was filed — states CWDI is tasked with developing the waterfront using a "community-first approach consistent with the community's long-term vision. It says the realization of that vision is threatened by the city's actions.
The press release says the city eliminated "baseless claims" that CWDI illegally transferred property from its amended lawsuit on May 3.
"Someone advising the city commissioners must have finally read all the transfer documents, and not just the one the city used in their original filing," CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said. "So they pulled that claim in their amended filing."
The press release also states that the amended lawsuit does not contain language asserting there could not be an imminent hotel deal.
The lawsuit filed May 1 mentions CWDI's "imminent" agreement with a boutique hotel developer, which Hengst said was nearing signing at a CWDI Board of Directors meeting March 20. The lawsuit states it is "highly unlikely" that the deal is imminent because "any established hotelier would conduct significant due diligence," which includes inquiring the city about various aspects of the project. The lawsuit says the city has not received any inquiries.
"Whoever advised the city commissioners that there was no way CWDI could have a hotel deal ready to sign clearly has no idea how property development works or community development or economic development," Leonard said in the press release.
Hengst said that with CWDI's response to the lawsuit filed May 14, the board hopes the city commissioners have all of the facts to withdraw the lawsuit "and return to a more collaborative path with us and the other partners."

title: Candidates vie for 3 Easton Town Council seats
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Candidates vie for 3 Easton Town Council seats

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: News 
 
 264
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton will hold a town election Tuesday, May 6, for three seats on the five-person Town Council. Residents can vote at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department on Leonard Rieck Drive from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.The council is made up of a president along with four representatives from the town's election wards.
For the council president seat, incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello will square off. Gunsallus has served as Town Council president since September 2023. Abbatiello has represented Ward 2 on the council since 2019.
With Abbatiello opting to run for president, a new resident will assume the Ward 2 seat. In that race, Lynnette Keefe and Robert Rankin will face off. Ward 2 includes a large portion of town east of U.S. Route 50 and north of Dutchman's Lane, as well as residents on the west side of the highway, south of Idlewild Avenue and east of Route 322.
The Ward 4 race will present voters with three options: incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, who has served in the seat since 2020; Moonyene Jackson-Amis, previously Ward 4's representative from 2001 to 2008; and Cameron Keefe. Ward 4 encompasses much of Easton's downtown area in between Routes 50 and 322, including residents north of Idlewild Avenue and on the east side of Aurora Street up past Dover Road.
The Star Democrat sent a questionnaire to all candidates running in the May 6 election to allow them to share their perspectives on various town issues in their own words.
Today's paper features the responses from the candidates for the Ward 2 race.

title: A LEGEND LOST - Orioles great and 16-time Gold Glove winner Brooks Robinson dies at 86
content:
A LEGEND LOST - Orioles great and 16-time Gold Glove winner Brooks Robinson dies at 86

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 40 | Section: Sports 
 
 1312
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE - Hall of Fame third baseman Brooks Robinson, whose deft glovework and folksy manner made him one of the most beloved and accomplished athletes in Baltimore history, has died. He was 86.The Orioles announced his death in a joint statement with Robinson's family Tuesday. The statement did not say how Robinson died.The Orioles held a moment of silence before their game against the Washington Nationals, and the teams lined up outside their dugouts to pay their respects.Also before the game, fans gathered around the 9-foot bronze statue of Robinson inside Camden Yards."Great player, great guy on the field, great guy off," said fellow Orioles Hall of Famer Jim Palmer, who was overcome with emotion."Respectful, kind. And you don't meet too many guys like that. Brooks was a genuine person. There was no acting. Brooks was just a genuine person."Coming of age before the free agent era, Robinson spent his entire 23-year career with the Orioles. He almost single-handedly helped Baltimore defeat Cincinnati in the 1970 World Series and homered in Game 1 of the Orioles' 1966 sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers for their first crown.Robinson participated in 18 All-Star Games, won 16 consecutive Gold Gloves and earned the 1964 AL Most Valuable Player award after batting .318 with 28 home runs and a league-leading 118 RBIs."An integral part of our Orioles Family since 1955, he will continue to leave a lasting impact on our club, our community, and the sport of baseball," the team said.He finished with 268 homers, drove in 1,357 runs and batted a respectable .267 in 2,896 career games. Not bad for ol' No. 5, the boy from Arkansas.MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred described Robinson as "one of the greats of our National Pastime.""Brooks stood among the greatest defensive players who have ever lived," Manfred said in a statement." He was a model of excellence, durability, loyalty and winning baseball for the Orioles."I will always remember Brooks as a true gentleman who represented our game extraordinarily well on and off the field all his life."MLB Player Association Executive Director Tony Clark cited Robinson's role as an advocate for his fellow players."Tributes to Brooks Robinson will duly note his brilliance at third base . But his impact transcended the field - as a prominent voice in the early days of the MLBPA and a relentless advocate for his fellow players through his work with the Major League Baseball Players Alumni Association. His humanity, kindness, integrity and commitment will long endure."The Hall of Fame applauded Robinson's role as a member of its board."For generations of fans, Brooks Robinson's talent on the field was surpassed only by his incredible character and integrity. His love of the Hall of Fame brightened Cooperstown, as did his devotion to the Museum as a long-standing and valued member of our Board of Directors."Robinson will be forever remembered for his work ethic and the skill he displayed at the hot corner, where he established himself as one of the finest fielding third baseman in baseball history, whether charging slow rollers or snaring liners down the third-base line."Brooks was maybe the last guy to get into the clubhouse the day of the game, but he would be the first guy on the field," former Orioles manager Earl Weaver said. "He'd be taking his groundballs, and we'd all go, 'Why does Brooks have to take any groundballs?' "I wouldn't expect anything else from Brooks. Seeing him work like that meant a lot of any young person coming up. He was so steady, and he steadied everybody else."Robinson arrived in Baltimore in September 1955 as an 18-yearold after spending most of his first professional season in baseball with Class B York. He went 2 for 22 with the Orioles and struck out 10 times.He jockeyed between the majors and minors until July 1959, when he stuck around in Baltimore for good."I think maybe he always knew what it's like to be in the big leagues at 19. And then I think when you get to the big leagues, you get here, you got to stay here, you got to figure out how to get better," Palmer said. "You have to decide who you want to be like. I think for all of us who knew him he was the best."Brooks Calbert Robinson Jr. was born in Little Rock on May 18, 1937. He eventually made Baltimore his home but never really lost his southern twang, which was just fine with fans in blue-collar Baltimore, who appreciated his homespun charm and unassuming demeanor.Dubbed "Mr. Oriole," he was a sports hero in Charm City, in the pantheon with former Colts quarterback Johnny Unitas and Orioles infielder Cal Ripken, who performed for a different generation.Many Orioles rooters who never got to see Robinson play still were able to enjoy his observations as he was part of team broadcasts.Ripken was known as The Iron Man because he played in 2,632 consecutive games, but Robinson wasn't fond of sitting on the bench, either. From 1960-1975, he played in at least 152 games in 14 seasons and in 144 games the other two years."I'm a guy who just wanted to see his name in the lineup everyday," he said. "To me, baseball was a passion to the point of obsession."Robinson retired in 1977 after batting only .149 in 24 games. His jersey was retired that year.Robinson's most memorable performance came as MVP of the 1970 World Series, when the Orioles bounced back from their stunning defeat to the New York Mets the year before and Robinson redeemed himself after batting just 1 for 19 in that series.Because he was so sensational in the field during Baltimore's fivegame triumph over the Reds, few remember he hit .429 and homered twice and drove in six runs - or that he made an error on his first play in the field.In Game 1, Robinson delivered the tiebreaking home run in the seventh inning. One inning earlier, he made a sensational backhanded grab of a hard grounder hit down the line by Lee May, spun around in foul territory and somehow threw out the runner.Robinson contributed an RBI single in the second game and became forever a part of World Series lore with his standout performance in Game 3. He made a tremendous, leaping grab of a grounder by Tony Perez to start a first-inning double play; charged a slow roller in the second inning and threw out Tommy Helms; then capped his memorable afternoon with a diving catch of a liner by Johnny Bench. The Series ended, fittingly, with a ground out to Robinson in Game 5, a 9-3 Orioles win."I'm beginning to see Brooks in my sleep," Reds manager Sparky Anderson said during the Series."If I dropped this paper plate, he'd pick it up on one hop and throw me out at first."Anderson also said, "He can throw his glove out there and it will start 10 double plays by itself."Palmer and other teammates would say that the country got to see what Robinson did routinely during the regular season. Robinson used to blush when asked to recall his heroics in October 1970."I tell people that I played 23 seasons and I never did have five games in a row like I did in that World Series," he said. "It was a once in a lifetime five-game series for me, and it just happened to be in a World Series."His legacy in Maryland continued long after his retirement.There's a Brooks Robinson Drive in Pikesville, and the annual state high school All-Star game played at Camden Yards is named in his honor.

title: Vote 'yes' on Question A — support public safety
author: PETE LESHER
content:
Vote 'yes' on Question A — support public safety

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PETE LESHER | Section: Columns 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Four years ago, Talbot County voters overwhelmingly approved a temporary increase in the property tax revenue cap by an "extra penny." Our public safety operations were facing a recruitment and retention crisis because of low pay and inferior benefits compared to surrounding jurisdictions.Talbot County has made enormous progress with the "extra penny" on the property tax since 2022. Sheriff's deputies' pay is competitive and sheriff's deputies now are on the state-sponsored LEOPS retirement program, allowing them to retire after 25 years. These benefits, in conjunction with solid leadership, means the Sheriff's Office can fill open positions. Deputies now retire from the department – a once-rare circumstance – rather than leaving to work in other jurisdictions.
Likewise, our Emergency Services compensation has increased.
Pay for paramedics, emergency medical technicians and 911 dispatchers is more competitive than in 2020 — though we need to monitor this against surrounding counties, and paramedics are now eligible for the LEOPS retirement program, a popular benefit. The county has stepped its sixth advanced life aupport ambulance crew to a seven-day, round-the-clock unit, helping us keep response times within the critical 8-minute standard.
The county is planning a new ambulance station near the Chapel District Elementary School, which will help reduce response times in the northeast corner of Talbot County, where we have struggled to meet the 8-minute standard.
Our County Detention Center has faced staffing shortages, forcing mandatory overtime to operate the facility safely. The County has responded by boosting correctional officer salaries and budgeted to convert their retirement plan to the more robust state-sponsored CORS program.
The state of Maryland mandates what we spend on our court system and the minimum that we must spend on public schools. While the state allows the county to exceed its property tax cap to fund schools, there is no state mandate to fund the sheriff's department or ambulance services or road repairs. And so these critical county services may suffer if the property tax cap restricts revenues and forces cuts.
All of the funds raised by the "extra penny" on the property tax since 2022 — and more — has gone to boosting public safety. The "extra penny" runs out in 2026. The Talbot County Council unanimously authorized a ballot question to renew the "extra penny" for seven more years, out of concern public safety costs will continue to rise faster than the 2% property tax cap.
Voting for Question A allows the County Council the option to levy the "extra penny" for seven more years — through fiscal year 2033. Even with this "extra penny," over the last four years or for the next seven years, Talbot County maintains the lowest property tax rate in the state of Maryland.
If you support public safety and emergency services, vote for Question A. Do it for your family's safety. Do it for your neighbors. Do it for your own good. Vote for Question A.

title: Pastoral Ponderings: The Lenten season
author: DANIEL T. GEDMAN St. Luke’s GMC
content:
Pastoral Ponderings: The Lenten season

 March 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DANIEL T. GEDMAN St. Luke’s GMC | Section: News 
 
 332
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Lenten season begins today, a day called Ash Wednesday.Ashes are a sign of mortality and repentance. The uses of ashes dates back to ancient Jewish tradition and often were associated with sacrifices, mourning and fasting. A person would properly express grief, humiliation and repentance sitting in ashes or placing them on the head.
At one time, during the early centuries of the church, public penitents at Rome were ceremonially admitted on this day to begin their penance.
This ceremony fell into disuse between the eighth and 10th centuries as general penance of the entire congregation began to take place. This penance was symbolized through the imposition of ashes.
Another use for ashes in the early church (second century) included a regular ceremony of public confession and penance. This use had acquired so much significance that Tertullian (a prolific early Christian author from Carthage in the Roman province of Africa) spoke of "the substitution of sackcloth and ashes for a man's usual habit."
Today, ashes symbolize the same meanings though the ceremonial customs have vanished. The one exception to this is Ash Wednesday.
The word "Lent" derives from the anglo-saxon term lencten, meaning "spring." During this time we earnestly recount all that God accomplished through the work of Jesus Christ.
We experience this period every year in the life of the church, but often, we forget, or sometimes we never knew what this time of year is about. Lent as a forty-day period of focus on penitence and preparation for the Resurrection Event of Easter. Today, we tend to observe Lent as a time of penance, by abstaining from festivals, by almsgiving, and by devoting more than the usual time to exercises of the faith. In recent years, more emphasis has been placed on these aspects than the physical fasting that marked this season in the early church.
I pray that this Lenten season would be a holy and sacred time of preparation for the celebration of the greatest day in human history; the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

 DENTON — Eden Town Brewing Company hopes to finish construction in August and open in the fall.A dream from husband and wife combo Matt and Sarah Dahl brought Edens Town Brewing Company to Denton. According to the business website, Matt and Sarah dreamed of building a family business in Denton for many years.
"My wife was born and raised here in Denton. We lived in North Carolina for a while, which is where I'm from, and down there, there's lots of breweries," Matt Dahl said. "We saw how much people loved breweries as a place to just come and get a beer or just hang out with friends and family.

title: Caroline County Board of Ed declares last day of school, discuss virtual instruction
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Board of Ed declares last day of school, discuss virtual instruction

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Caroline County Board of Education declared Tuesday, June 17, as the last day of the extended school year after inclement weather closures exceeded the four days allotted.The last day will be a half day for students and a full day for teachers.
Next year, county schools will have three allotted inclement weather days. At the April 1 Board of Education meeting, district officials explored options for implementing virtual instruction should weather cause unexpected closures.
Because of the challenges presented by district officials, the board concluded it thinks the district will not be able to conduct virtual instruction on inclement weather days.
"The structure we tried to take with the presentation was a condensed version of some the requirements that the school system would have to meet if the county were to entertain virtual weather days," Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons said. "We walked through some real tough spots for us to get to those points."
Internet Connection and Google Meets
There are multiple factors Caroline County board of education most consider to conduct virtual inclement weather days. Including ensuring every student has a hotspot or wifi to participate in virtual learning.
Robert Wielgosz, supervisor of technology, led the discussion on cellular service, offering points on the Kajeet program.
Kajeet was a hotspot used during the pandemic for students to connect to the internet in areas where wifi access was limited and not available.
According to Wielgosz, when given the opportunity to use Kajeet, some students would use the hotspot for personal uses like video games and movies. This overloaded the hotspots and caused delays.
The estimate cost for Caroline County to provide the 700 needed Kajeet devices over five years would be about $736,000 for students and $35,000 for teachers.
Wielgosz also mentioned the need for Google Meet Breakout Rooms, which teachers use to conduct learning activities with groups in virtual classrooms. While this feature was available at no cost, it is no longer available in Caroline County's free Google plan.
"To get the feature back, it's going to cost Caroline County somewhere between $30,000 to $50,000 a year to get the premium Google aspect," Wielgosz said.
Multilingual Learners, Special Education and Homelessness
State law mandates districts "ensure that all staff and students, including students with disabilities, homeless students, and English language learners, have the necessary devices at home for virtual education days, including access to Wifi."
Providing equitable access to these services can be challenging during virtual instruction, district officials said.
Caroline County has 576 multilingual learners, 569 individualized education program students and 116 students who experience homelessness. For these students, hands-on teacher engagement and preparation is required for proper learning.
"It's very hard to keep students engaged, especially for four hours of synchronous instruction," Erica McDonald, supervisor of special education, said. "Without that in-person tangible motivating things that can keep them engaged during instruction, it can lead to increased frustration."
Providing necessary technologies and translation services are also complicated by virtual instruction, the officials said.
Teacher, staff negotiations
Some district employees work on inclement weather days, and some staff members do not work and still get paid, district officials said.
Requirements of the state say, "during virtual inclement weather days the local school system shall offer public school employees who are not assigned to work during the virtual education day an opportunity to make up the lost work through other duties before the beginning of the next school year."
The district would be responsible for determining how this work would be made up.
Virtual learning days require additional planning from teachers, which requires a negotiation with the teachers' union for proper pay.
"Our teachers work really hard. We all know are teachers work outside of hours. We have all come to accept that it comes with the job," Dr. Robert Willoughby, director of administrative services said. "However, the law does say that we may negotiate with our teachers' union. They have a right to come to negotiate if there is extra work here we would like extra compensation for that."
After going through the presentation, Simmons concluded it would be to hard for the county to pull off virtual inclement weather days.
"I don't see how as a county, with the resources we have right now, that this puts us in a great position to be able to hit all the marks to be able to pull this off effectively to meet all requirements," Simmons said.

title: Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 976
 Words 

 Read News Document

 City officials in Newark, Delaware are in the early stages of evaluating whether a transitional housing village of small cabins could be a solution to local homelessness.Council members John Suchanec and Corinth Ford visited such a village in Georgetown, Delaware and suggested that a similar idea could be implemented here.
"We truly felt the experience was transformative," Suchanec said. "The approach that Georgetown has taken is starting to shape up to be a model for how you would deal with homeless sheltering."
Georgetown's Pallet Village was built in 2023 by the nonprofit Springboard Delaware. It consists of 40 small one-bedroom cabins, as well as shared bathhouses. It's become known as the Pallet Village because the cabins are produced by a company called Pallet.
"Our goal is to get unsheltered people out of the woods, get the help they need and move on to permanent housing or some form of self-independence," said Judson Malone, executive director of Springboard Delaware.
Malone said there are many reasons that people stay in the woods rather than go into traditional homeless shelters. Maybe they don't feel safe in a group shelter, they can't be with their partner, they can't bring their pet or they can't bring all their possessions.
"The most impactful thing you will do for them immediately is a lockable door with heat and air conditioning in a secure community, and that's exactly what we provided," Malone said. "Within two weeks, you'll see a difference in their demeanor simply because of the trauma that they experienced in the woods."
The Pallet Village does not require residents to be sober.
"We do not allow substance use on site, but best practices have shown that when people are in a safe space where they're accepted as they are, they can then begin to process the other issues in their life, including deciding whether or not to get treatment," Malone said. "We have a very high success rate of people voluntarily choosing to go to treatment."
Within a week of opening, the Georgetown shelter was 100 percent occupied and has remained so.
"People see a value in being there," Malone said. "They want to be there, and they want to get help and support."
Springboard Delaware works with 30 different support organizations to provide medical, mental heath, banking, employment and other services to people living at the Pallet Village.
"While people are unsheltered and in the woods, they almost never want those services," Malone said. "They really don't care about getting clean or sober, because getting high is how they survive a traumatic life."
The average length of stay is approximately three months, and then many residents of the Pallet Village move on to more permanent housing.
The Pallet Village cost approximately $1.5 million to build, money that came from the American Rescue Plan Act. Ongoing funds for operation has been harder to come by, however. Last year, Springboard Delaware had to lay off staff when a grant fell through and leaders were scrambling to piece together state money and private grants to keep the village open, according to reporting from Spotlight Delaware.
Malone said he is still working with the state to develop sustainable longterm funding.
Springboard Delaware has another $1.4 million in ARPA money to build a second Pallet Village somewhere else in the state.
"We've got the money in hand to do it," Malone said. "We just need a location."
If a Pallet Village were built in Newark, it would not require funding from the city, Malone said.
Ultimately, Springboard Delaware envisions building five to seven Pallet Villages around the state by the end of the decade.
"We have a vision, and we believe that homelessness is solvable," Malone said. "This is not the whole solution, but it's a huge part of it."
During a city council meeting last month, several council members expressed skepticism.
"Obviously, we all want to be compassionate, we all want to be empathetic, and we all want to help solve this problem," Mayor Travis McDermott said. "But we have realistic hurdles that we would have to overcome, and even with our best intentions, we can't escape it."
One big question, he said, is where would a Pallet Village be located.
"People are not going to want you to use the land behind their house to build this," McDermott said. "That's just a simple fact."
Councilman Jay Bancroft expressed similar thoughts.
"I hope we'll be very sensitive to local opposition that is likely to be an issue," Bancroft said. "I think this idea of making it look suitable to the neighbors is important for this education campaign, for us to take steps that we've been talking about for a long time"
Councilman Jason Lawhorn noted that the Georgetown Pallet Village was built near where there was already a large established homeless encampment. He said it's important to understand the scale of homelessness in Newark to better understand whether a Pallet Village would be utilized here.
He added that city staffers are already overworked and questioned whether the city should have a role in creating a Pallet Village.
"I love the program," he said. "I have reservations about how we execute it in Newark."
Suchanec asked his colleagues to direct City Manager Tom Coleman to prepare a report on whether there are any city-owned properties that could potentially be used for a Pallet Village. He suggested looking at underutilized parks as well as a piece of land the city recently purchased off Paper Mill Road, between the city's electric substation and White Clay Creek.
Ultimately, the council decided that in order to not burden city employees, each council member will compile of list of possible locations in their district for further study.
"You can find so many reasons to say no for something," Suchanec said. "The easy thing is to say no or to convince yourself this is something not worth doing. All I'm saying is take a baby step. Find out if we have any locations in this city where something like this could happen."

title: Larry L. O'Ferrall
content:
Larry L. O'Ferrall

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 LANHAM - Larry Lee O'Ferrall passed away on December 5, 2023 at the age of 84 with his family by his side. He was born near East New Market in 1939, to the late Margaret and William O'Ferrall. Larry had three brothers Franklin, William, and Daniel O'Ferrall. He attended North Dorchester High School and graduated in 1957.Larry married Helen Hurlock on August 7, 1960 in Hurlock, MD. They moved to the suburbs of Washington, DC and in 1966, they had a son, Larry Allen O'Ferrall. Larry Lee has two grandchildren, Steven and Shannon O'Ferrall.
Larry worked in the computer field for the Central Intelligence Agency from 1960 to 2005. After retiring he briefly worked for the US Army as a contractor.
Larry was an avid sports fan who played baseball and football in High School as well as softball and football with the CIA. For over a decade he played softball on the same team with his son.
He was an avid reader and interested in history.
He enjoyed crabbing and fishing in the rivers on the Eastern Shore as a youth. He was a devoted family man and a proud grandparent. He was always in attendance at his grandchildren's events and games.
Besides his wife Helen, Larry is survived by Larry Allen O'Ferrall, his daughter-in-law Elizabeth O'Ferrall, his grandchildren Steven and Shannon O'Ferrall, his sister-in-law Barbara O'Ferrall and several nieces and nephews. He is preceded in death by his parents and brothers.
A viewing and funeral service will be held at the Zeller Funeral Home in East New Market, MD on Sunday, December 17th. The viewing will be at 1 pm and service at 2 pm. The burial will follow immediately at the Unity Washington Cemetery in Hurlock.

title: For All Seasons gives update on human trafficking in Talbot County
author: Konner Metz
content:
For All Seasons gives update on human trafficking in Talbot County

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Representatives from For All Seasons say the problem of human trafficking in Talbot County is persisting, though they are seeing positive gains in awareness and detection.During a Talbot County Council meeting Tuesday, Lauren Weber, the nonprofit's vice president of strategy and development, provided an update to council members regarding human and labor trafficking.
"It is happening and it's happening here. That continues to be the case," Weber said. " … There's a complexity to human trafficking that it doesn't really know county boundaries."
Weber and Katie Theeke, vice president of marketing and communications, each said the organization has a special role given its wide reach. For All Seasons' presence in the five Mid-Shore counties — Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot — is critical to providing victims with essential services.
"We know that human trafficking knows no boundaries and that it affects people of different backgrounds, races, genders," Theeke said. "We have seen several cases come through our doors, and it comes from Talbot County. It comes from neighboring counties. We really aim to be the connector to get those people the help that they need."
Council Member Keasha Haythe asked if For All Seasons is seeing a decline in human trafficking numbers. Weber said it's a "double-edged sword."
"A year ago we sat in front of you and said, when we look at our rape crisis center data, a good fifth of what was coming in was having at least one indicator of human trafficking," Weber said. " … That persists."
The organization has noticed a shift in how many people are recognizing signs of human trafficking and making those reports, Weber says.
"The folks that are self-referring, we're seeing a decline," she said. "But we're seeing a real rapid incline in folks coming to us and saying, 'Hey, I know more and now I've seen something.'"
Weber said that since September, more than 120 people have taken For All Seasons' free, online anti-human trafficking course.
For All Seasons is an official regional navigator for the Mid-Shore area, Theeke said, meaning it works on task forces and serves youth and young adults that are victims of trafficking.
At the end of the discussion, council members thanked the For All Seasons representatives for their work and presented the organization with a proclamation Tuesday declaring January as National Human Trafficking Awareness Month.
"We know that even one victim is too many," council Vice President Pete Lesher said. "We appreciate all that you do both on prevention, but also to develop and take care of those who have been victims."

 EASTON - Angie Webb wasn't sure what she did.But Saints Peter and Paul High's freshman knew the way her field hockey teammates were celebrating it must have been something good.It also proved to be the difference Tuesday, as Webb ripped the game's lone goal into the right side of the cage with 3:50 remaining in the first quarter, helping the Sabres to a 1-0 victory over Easton."It was a beautiful goal," Sts. Peter & Paul head coach Debbie McQuaid said after the Sabres improved to 10-2 with their fourth straight victory, the last three by shutout.Webb gained possession of the ball from about 25 yards away from Easton's cage near the 4-minute mark of the first period. She circled left, then moved right before unloading a hard drive from the left side that got past Warrior goalie Alli Newman before banging into the far right corner of the cage."My teammates basically helped us all get up the field," Webb said. "I just took it and I don't know what really happened.I was just really determined to get that goal. I knew I had to get off a shot real quickly. I just hit it and it went in. I was really shocked." Easton (5-4) earned two of its nine penalty corners in the final 1:15 of the first quarter, getting one shot off that was wide of the mark. Both teams each picked up one corner in the second quarter, but could not capitalize.The game remained even through the third, as the Warriors picked up three more corners, with Easton's Bis Johnson firing wide left.Sts. Peter & Paul had one corner in the third, with Gennie Webb shooting wide right."They came out and they scored on us, and it was a beautiful goal," said Easton head coach Kim Neff, whose team lost its second straight by shutout. "I do feel like the rest of the game we picked up our pace, we had good passing.I felt like our defense and middies played a really great game."They just struck first and we just couldn't capitalize on our opportunities," Neff continued."We had plenty of corners. We had plenty of shots. We just couldn't put it in today." The Sabres earned their fourth and final corner with 11 minutes remaining but didn't managed anything on goal. Easton had two more corner chances, the last with a minute remaining but could not get the equalizer."We really had the determination to win," Sts. Peter & Paul's Jules Stepp said. "They're our friends, and even though they're our friends, we like to have our friendly competition with them."I really think we communicated well and we looked up and we passed to each other," Stepp continued. "And we played a little bit of short and long ball together. And our defense, every time they got the opportunity to get the ball they cleared it out to the side and they recovered. They were on their 'A' game today." But McQuaid thought it took a little while for that 'A' game to materialize."Defense held solid," said McQuaid after goalie Maddie Maloney and company registered their sixth shutout of the season. "They were a little befuddled in the first half and not marking the way they were supposed to. It took them until the second half to start marking the way they were supposed to.Both teams played hard. Lot of skill on both sides.K. content:
TODAY IN HISTORY/April 15

 April 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Columns 
 
 338
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On April 15, 1912, the British luxury liner RMS Titanic sunk in the North Atlantic off Newfoundland just over two and a half hours after hitting an iceberg on its maiden voyage. More than 1,500 people died; 710 survived.Also on this date:
In 1865, Abraham Lincoln died after being shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theater the previous evening; Andrew Johnson was sworn in as the 17th president hours later.
In 1947, Jackie Robinson, baseball's first Black major league player of the modern era, made his official debut with the Brooklyn Dodgers on opening day at Ebbets Field. (The Dodgers defeated the Boston Braves, 5-3.)
In 1955, Ray Kroc opened the first franchised McDonald's restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois.
In 1974, members of the Symbionese Liberation Army held up a branch of the Hibernia Bank in San Francisco; a member of the group was SLA kidnap victim Patricia Hearst. (Hearst later said she had been forced to participate in the robbery.)
In 1989, a crush of soccer fans at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, England, caused 97 deaths and over 760 injuries.
In 2013, two bombs made from pressure cookers exploded at the Boston Marathon finish line, killing two women and an 8-year-old boy and injuring more than 260.
In 2019, fire swept across the top of the Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral during renovation work on the landmark structure; the blaze collapsed the cathedral's spire and spread to one of its iconic rectangular towers. (The cathedral was restored and reopened to the public in December 2024.)
Today's Birthdays: Actor Claudia Cardinale is 87. Basketball Hall of Famer Michael Cooper is 69. Olympic track and field gold medalist Evelyn Ashford is 68. Actor-screenwriter Emma Thompson is 66. title: GREENSBORO CANDIDATE: Paula Turner
author: Staff Writer
content:
GREENSBORO CANDIDATE: Paula Turner

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Caroline 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PAULA TURNERAge: 54Family: Mother of two successful grown daughters, 2 great son-in-laws and GiGi to 4 of the world's cutest and most amazing grandchildren.
Education: 1989 Kent Co High School Graduate
Occupation: Licensed Life and Health Insurance Agent; I also have a background in banking and investments.
Previous political experience: None.
1. Why are you running for Greensboro Town Council?
Trust me, this was not planned or even an aspiration of mine however, once I started seeing my responsibilities as a homeowner becoming more costly with nothing changing for the better, I began attending town council meetings. I found like minded people asking the same questions.The more I showed up and listened, I realized that we've been going around in circles, with no improvement in sight. I finally decided to be a part of the change that I'd like to see.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
To ensure that the most qualified people are employed by our town and ensure they have what they need to be productive and successful. To call for accountability of rental landlords and property owners on the upkeep and condition of their properties. If anyone needs help, we guide them to the resources they need. Sending out fines to already struggling families only causes hard feelings and more trust issues. Create and maintain safe neighborhoods by working with & alongside the Greensboro Police Department.
3. Transparency with the residents has been questioned by Greensboro residents. How would you plan to be transparent with the residents?
Through honesty and respect, by allowing the community to have a voice in decisions that directly affect them. I would like to create a monthly/quarterly newsletter (put together by volunteers) that would include a calendar of events, our meeting dates/times, church services and our food pantry schedule.
4. Multiple solar projects have been proposed for Caroline County. What rules should Greensboro have in place for these projects?
Unfortunately you are asking this question a few months too late. I petitioned the courts along with 2 other residents to block Halo from being able to move into our town but because those that came before us and not looking ahead, we lost. We will need to look outside of the box and stay up on the local and state happenings so that we can stay ahead of the curve. Thinking that "it won't happen here" has not done our town much good.
