title: QAC achieves significant milestone in reducing marine industry plastic waste
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QAC achieves significant milestone in reducing marine industry plastic waste

 July 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County has achieved a remarkable success in its ongoing efforts to reduce plastic waste generated by the marine industry. The county's recent initiative to recycle single-use boat shrink wrap has resulted in a significant increase in the amount of plastic diverted from landfills.In the second year of the program, the Queen Anne's County government, in partnership with Plastic Free QAC and the Marine Trades Association of Maryland, has seen a 370% increase in the amount of recycled shrink wrap compared to last year.
This year, a total of six tons pounds of plastic shrink wrap was collected and recycled, a substantial increase from the 1.62 tons collected in 2023.
Queen Anne's County Commissioner Phil Dumenil expressed his enthusiasm, stating, "This significant increase in our recycling efforts underscores the dedication and commitment of our residents and businesses to protect our county. By expanding the availability of MTAM recycle bags and increasing the public awareness, we have made it easier for everyone to participate in this important initiative."
Key highlights of this year's success include:
Increased participation from individual boat owner with a notable rise in the number of individual boat owners participating in the recycling program, showcasing the community's growing environmental consciousness.Expansion of recycling bag pickup locations; the program expanded from one to four convenient pickup locations for MTAM recycle bags, including:West Marine in Chester, Rommel's Ace Hardware in Stevensville, Centreville Town Hall and Refill Goodness in Stevensville.Commitment from local marinas and boat companies. Several local businesses committed to responsible disposal of shrink wrap, among them: Bay Bridge Marina, Bosun's Marine, Atlantic Yacht Services and Pocket Yacht Company
The MTAM recycle bags, sponsored by the County Commissioners, were provided free of charge and made available at multiple locations. The dedicated MTAM shrink wrap dumpster at the Grasonville Transfer Station facilitated easy and eco-friendly disposal for boat owners from early April to June.
This initiative is part of Queen Anne's County's broader commitment to environmental stewardship and sustainability. By continuing to work together, the county aims to set an example for other communities across Maryland and beyond.
Plastic Free QAC started in 2018 with the mission to reduce single-use plastic usage in general and places focus on education and building public awareness, according to Sara Shelley, president of Plastic Free QAC.
"We are really thrilled with the community response," she said.
Understanding that old habits with single-use plastics can be hard to shake, Plastic Free QAC looks to continually build involvement by connecting with individual boat owners and hosting community-wide clean ups, Shelley said.
For more information about the recycling program, including where to pick up MTAM recycle bags and drop off cleaned shrink wrap, visit https://lnk.bio/RecycleBoatShrinkwrap.

title: As avian flu spreads, local businesses grapple with increased egg costs
author: Konner Metz
content:
As avian flu spreads, local businesses grapple with increased egg costs

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 460
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Steve Mangasarian's is paying double what he used to for wholesale eggs.He says the price has been rising steadily since the pandemic. The recent spread of avian influenza virus, or avian flu, is accelerating that trend.
Mangasarian, the owner and chef of Breakfast in Easton, buys eggs from a vendor that sources locally. Due to the avian flu threatening poultry flocks nationwide, egg shortages are impacting businesses.
"The entire supply, nationwide supply, has been curtailed because of this. There's a shortage, even though I'm using local, fresh eggs," Mangasarian said. "Everybody's getting squeezed."
Mangasarian, like some other business owners, has been forced to raise prices. At Breakfast in Easton, he's added a 50-cent surcharge to an order of eggs and a 75-cent surcharge to an order of pancakes.
"It is my intention to make this temporary," signs in the restaurant read.
Avian flu outbreaks across the nation have afflicted egg supply, with the worst impacts felt in western and midwestern states. But local flocks have been affected as well.
Per the Maryland Department of Agriculture, five commercial poultry farms on the Eastern Shore have experienced outbreaks, including three just last month. Several other cases were reported in Delaware.
The virus can spread easily between flocks, though the risk for bird-to-human transmission is low at present.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average cost for a dozen eggs was $4.15 at the end of 2024. One year earlier, the average cost was $2.51.
The current mark is nearing record costs seen during the avian flu outbreak in 2022. And U.S. Department of Agriculture projections predict a 20% increase in egg prices for 2025.
For Mangasarian, the sharp rise in egg prices has been a significant challenge. In past years, lower egg wholesale prices helped him "subsidize" a low return on bacon. That's flipped, however, as his returns on bacon now make up for tight egg returns.
At the Easton Diner on U.S. Route 50, manager Tiff Haddaway says it costs around $1,000 more per week to purchase eggs due to the recent shortage and wholesale prices. As of now, customers aren't seeing an upcharge.
"The owner is trying to not pass it onto the customer," Haddaway said.
Steve Andrews, owner of the Bagery, says customers aren't experiencing any increases since the business' local, free-range producer hasn't been hit by the avian flu.
Andrews, a backyard chicken flock owner for more than 15 years, did note that egg production costs have risen in past years due to increasing feed prices.
"We foresee that all producers, which get their day-old chicks from just a handful of operations, will all be increasing their demand to replace the culled flocks," Andrews wrote. "If any of the hatcheries themselves have an outbreak, this could indicate that egg prices have not peaked and could rise even further."

title: Men For Change recognizes volunteers' service
author: Tom McCall

Men For Change recognizes volunteers' service

 July 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On July 20, about 80 people gathered at the Federalsburg Volunteer Fire Company banquet hall to recognize Men For Change's People of the Year.The Federalsburg nonprofit's slogan is "changing our community through service." They are geared toward mentoring youth and trying to help them make productive choices. This was the 14th year of the recognition awards.
There were six people honored for their work: Federalsburg's District One Councilman Brandy James, Principal of Federalsburg Elementary School Stephanie Brohawn, coach and volunteer William Eric Smith, community activist Cynthia Fletcher, Haitian community liaison Cederick Turner and Roberta Butler of the NAACP.
Betty Jarman, the media spokesperson for Men For Change, said, "The keynote speaker for this event was Vaughn Evans Sr. He was the principal of the North Dorchester Middle School in Hurlock.
She said, "The Men For Change theme this year was 'Let's Get Busy,'" which featured heavily in Evans' address.
In his speech, Evans urged the audience to get busy doing productive, positive things to support youth with the resources they need to become successful.
"They are our future leaders and enterprising entrepreneurs," he said.
He said that the essence of his message aligns with Colossians 3:23-24, which encourages community service and giving back. The bible verse starts, "And whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord and not to men."
James, whose son was in the program years ago, said she is something of a "behind the scenes person" for the nonprofit.
"I am just part of a puzzle, and it takes more than me to push the wheel. It is a community effort," she said. "It was exciting to be acknowledged, but it was more exciting and more rewarding to see the others who were acknowledged.
"So much greatness being acknowledged — magnificent work. It is because of those individuals that so much goodness is happening in Federalsburg," James said.
Recognizing these volunteers is part of MFC's mission. They want the community to know what is happening.
"This is important because we want the broader community to know the people that are doing outstanding volunteer, work without any fanfare. These people are not looking for recognition. We want them to know that we appreciate the work that they are doing," Jarman said.
State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) made citations for all the honorees, though he was unable to attend the event in person.
A recent graduate who participated in the program was also honored Saturday evening. 2024 Colonel Richardson High School graduate Elson Davis was presented with a certificate.
Jarman said, "The event was well attended by young people, young Black men. I thought that was a wonderful thing that they were there to support the honorees."
Jarman also took the opportunity to highlight an upcoming partnership between Men for Change and another local organization, the Federalsburg Activity Center.
"We are also partnering with the Federalsburg Activity Center and their after school mentoring program and other activities going on at the center," Jarman said. "It is still in construction, but we hope it will be open by September."
This project, still under construction, is repurposing the Dollar General in Federalsburg. Men For Change is still open to receiving donations.
"Once the center is open, we will need more volunteers," Jarman said.

title: Lions survive Easton rally for title
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Lions survive Easton rally for title

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Jeff Hollis said he wasn't nervous, especially with seniors Vince Gilberto and Collin Woolford in the game."I always feel like with Vince and Collin on the court that somebody's going to make a winning play," said Hollis, Queen Anne's County High's boys head basketball coach.
Hollis was right. Somebody did make a winning play, and that somebody was freshman Jadereon Thompson.
Fouled with 1 second left, Thompson hit the first of two free throws Tuesday night to lift top-seeded Queen Anne's to a 66-65 victory over No. 2 seed Easton in the Class 2A East Region II championship.
The Lions (18-4), who have won six straight since a Jan. 30 loss at Easton, now wait for the Class 2A field to be reseeded, and will likely host a state quarterfinal either Friday or Saturday. Easton finishes the season 15-7.
"Really elated. It's been three years coming to this game and we've lost two of them," said Hollis, whose season was ended by Wicomico the past two years in the region final. "So to finally win one feels really good."
Down 32-31 at halftime, the Lions looked well on their way to victory as they outscored Easton, 22-7, in the third quarter to carry a 53-39 lead into the fourth.
But behind Marshall Bailey, who scored 17 of his game-high 27 points in the fourth quarter, Easton rallied as the sophomore guard scored on a drive with 4 seconds remaining to tie the game at 65-65.
On the ensuing inbounds pass, Gilberto threw a pass three-quarters of the court to Thompson, who drove straight to the basket and was fouled with 1 second left on the clock.
"I was either going to get the layup or get fouled," Thompson said.
During a timeout prior to his free-throw attempts, Thompson said all his teammates came up to him offering him encouragement.
"It felt great," Thompson said. "I had to knock 'em down to win the regional final."
Thompson hit the first, then watched the second attempt bounce and get rebounded by Gilberto to seal the win.
"He's really not a freshman," Hollis said of Thompson. "He's a freshman in age, but he's not a freshman. He's been building to this point. He's just an exceptional kid and an exceptional athlete."
Easton outscored the Lions 26-13 in the fourth quarter.
"I thought we were going to overtime," Warrior head coach Dionte Hynson said. "I'm proud of the kids. Helluva comeback. We had to dig deep. We had to play solid D. I'm not taking anything away from Queen Anne's but our kids played their butts off tonight."
Diontye Copper's 3-pointer with 6:27 left in the third quarter pulled Easton even with the Lions at 35-all. But Queen Anne's outscored the Warriors 18-4 over the final 5:39 of the quarter to build a 53-39 lead, with Woolford (12 points) scoring seven points in the run.
"We just couldn't score any points third quarter," Hynson said.
Bailey, who was 8 of 9 from the foul line, hit a pair of free throws to start Easton's fourth-quarter comeback, drained two 3-pointers and continuously attacked the rim, scoring or drawing contact.
"He's a great player," Hollis said of Bailey. "Hat's off to Easton. I thought their players and their coaching staff did a great job. They weathered the storm when we got up on 'em. They came back.
"But our kids made the final winning play," Hollis added. "We talk about it all the time. Things happen during a game. Who's going to be the man that makes the final winning play. We've had that a couple times this year."
Gilberto had 14 points for Queen Anne's, Nickai Gross and Hollace Branch each had 10, and Thompson finished with nine.
Rayan Haq had 10 for Easton and Kyree Acree eight.

title: Moore says budget will balance, protect school funding
author: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service
content:
Moore says budget will balance, protect school funding

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 930
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore unveiled a budget proposal on Wednesday that would balance the books and protect the state's ambitious reform plan for Maryland public schools, without raising taxes in the fiscal year that begins in July.The $63.1 billion plan would balance the books where officials had projected a shortfall, in part by returning some programs to spending levels closer to those of the pre-pandemic era. The plan proposes leveraging state debt and dipping into rainy day funds.
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's sweeping education plan of 2021, will be fully funded, state budget officials said Wednesday. Moore, a Democrat, said his administration crafted the budget plan in partnership with lawmakers, community leaders and other "village elders."
"We wanted to make sure that this proposed budget had everyone's fingerprints on it," Moore said in his public announcement of the new plan. "Because this budget is not just a reflection of an administration. This budget is a reflection of our shared aspiration."
Those aspirations will now go to the Maryland General Assembly for debate. Lawmakers have set a target of early April for passing a budget, and the state Constitution requires that it be balanced.
But the joint Republican Caucus will look closely at where funding transfers in the proposed budget are coming from, House Minority Leader Jason Buckel, R-Allegany, told Capital News Service.
While he said he is pleased that the Moore administration kept total spending similar to that of years past, he expressed concerns about the possibility of fees for certain businesses or tax hikes down the road. Buckel said he'll keep worrying about that possibility until the legislature adjourns.
"All in all, it's a mixed bag, I think, and we'll look forward to working with the governor and working with the Democratic leadership here to try to make the budget as good as possible," Buckel said.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey suggested he worries about the possibility of fee increases down the road.
"While it is a relief that the governor's budget spends less than last year and does not raise taxes, the number of fee increases proposed by his administration through legislation and the regulatory process is concerning," said Hershey, a Republican representing Kent, Cecil, Queen Anne's and Caroline, in an email release. He and other Republicans contend fee hikes are coming through the administrative pipeline.
"Taxes aren't the only way to raise revenue," Hershey said, "and state government should not be in the business of nickel and diming Maryland's families and small businesses."
The only fee increases currently in the budget plan are in the Department of the Environment, and those would generate roughly $3.5 million in revenue, according to a spokesman for the governor's office.
Working together to approve a balanced budget had been shaping up as no easy task. The state's spending had been projected to outpace revenues starting in the coming fiscal year, according to a recent report from the Department of Legislative Services.
But Moore has now proposed a plan that would instead balance the 2025 budget, saying it is a step in the right direction toward addressing the state's structural deficit in the years beyond that.
His budget flips the expected cash shortfall of $1.1 billion to a positive cash balance of $103 million in fiscal 2025, according to Helene Grady, Maryland's secretary of budget and management.
Moore said his budget prioritizes public safety, affordable housing, child care, education and public service. It also raises pay for state employees.
"We know that budgets, they're moral documents," Moore said. "Where we choose to invest actually defines our values. And it dictates the course of our future."
State budget officials said they avoided wide-ranging cuts across the board, hiring freezes or salary freezes. Rather, state agency heads went through an intense process and found areas to trim, and several agency budgets will be lower this year than they were the year before.
Moore said he proposed a record $127 million for local police agencies, citing the importance of supporting law enforcement and getting "more boots on the ground" to solve crimes and keep repeat offenders off the streets. Other investments would go toward the prevention of gun violence and support for crime victims.
While addressing public safety, Moore acknowledged the debates about juvenile justice likely to come during the legislative session, announcing an increase in funding to the Department of Juvenile Services. He didn't specifically discuss any cuts made to juvenile services programs.
Affordable housing and child care would receive significant funding under the proposal. Those are two areas Moore claimed are the biggest strains on Maryland residents. Access to housing and child care allow for increased participation in the workforce as Maryland tries to grow its economy, he argued.
"Access to child care doesn't just affect your child and your family," Moore said. "It changes the trajectory of our state's fiscal health."
Options for job training in innovative industries and public service were a priority. Through Moore's budget, the state is on track to increase the number of Service Year Option and Maryland Corps participants to 500, as required by law.
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future will be fully funded in the coming fiscal year, budget officials said, but its money problems are far from resolved. Prior to the beginning of the legislative session, the Department of Legislative Services report projected the state would exhaust the Blueprint balance in fiscal 2027.
"It's not inaccurate to say, 'Hey, we funded the Blueprint, or at least the state's portion of the Blueprint, for today,'" Buckel said. "But I also think it's completely honest to say the blueprint looming large over the next four or five years, blows billion-dollar holes into our state budget."

Police investigating shooting in Greensboro

 GREENSBORO — Police are investigating a shooting that happened at a grocery store in Greensboro Wednesday afternoon.The shooting occurred around 3:30 p.m. in the parking lot of Save A Lot on Greensboro Road, according to the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.
Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer told The Star Democrat that as of Wednesday evening, the Sheriff's Office hadn't identified any injured victims or received calls from anyone with gunshot wounds.
Investigators checked surveillance videos, which showed "some type of exchange in the parking lot," Helmer said. County police, the Greensboro Police Department and Maryland State troopers were on the scene.
In a Thursday morning press release, authorities said that after the exchange, one person fled the scene while another gave chase and fired rounds from a handgun.
"After the gunfire, the unknown suspect fled in a dark-colored passenger car heading north on Greensboro Road, while another individual walked away towards (Whiteleysburg) Road," the press release stated.
Police are still working to identify a suspect, Helmer said. In a Facebook post, the Sheriff's Office said the shooting "is believed to be an isolated incident."
Anyone with information regarding the shooting may call 410-479-2515.

title: rest of mike's story
author: Staff Writer
content:
rest of mike's story

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Rest Of Mikes Story

 Read News Document

 FOCUS ON THE BASERyan Waite, a veteran campaign consultant and vice president of public affairs with northern California-based consulting firm Think Big, said the political parties and most campaigns are focused on ginning up and turning out their voter bases and don't tend to engage with low-propensity voters."They put resources where it is going to make the most difference. Typically, you are looking at people who have previously voted, who are kind in that soft middle," said Waite, who has mostly worked on Republican campaigns.
Waite said while social media can help engage more voters and could help engage nonvoters, especially young ones, the medium presents challenges.
"You are competing with everything else. The slice of time you get in front of them is very very small," he said of the social media content streams.
Negative campaigning, coarse social discourse and misinformation on key issues have also magnified on social media leaving voters and nonvoters distrustful of content and disparate and sometimes ideological information sources.
"It's hard for average voters to figure out what's going on," said Waite.
In an Aug. 26 letter to the House Judiciary Committee, META Platforms chairman and CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the Biden-Harris administration "repeatedly pressured" Facebook and Instagram to censor dissenting content (including humor and satire) related to COVID-19.
The White House defended those actions as helping protect public health from misinformation.
Recent surveys show low levels of trust in politics, the media and government, as well as plenty of economic stress stemming from the post-pandemic inflation wave.
A June survey by financial firm Credit Karma and research firm Qualtrics found 68% of Americans don't believe official economic data touting job gains and easing inflation after post-pandemic spikes in prices.
Another recent poll by Gallup and the Walton Foundation shows Gen Zers (ages 12 to 27) have little trust in the media, government and politics. But they showed strong turnout in 2020 and are expected to also show up in November, said Craig Snyder, campaign director for Haley Voters for Harris (a group that hopes to get GOP supporters of former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley to eschew Trump).
NEW ENERGY?Snyder said Harris' campaign should energize younger voters more than the matchup between Trump and President Joe Biden.
"They weren't excited about a race between two 80-year-old men," said Snyder, noting that Democratic enthusiasm for Harris will also generate GOP energy for Trump.
Harris was installed at the top of the Democratic ticket after Biden, 81, was pressured to quit the race by donors and party power players over concerns about his age.
Snyder said voting groups such as suburban women, Black and Hispanic men, along with voters on both sides of Israel's war in Gaza against Hamas could tip the race in battlegrounds such as Michigan, Wisconsin, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.
Independent presidential candidate Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s endorsement of Trump could also shift his voters, many of whom are disaffected by COVID policies (including vaccines), in key states.
Snyder also sees another contingent of nonvoters beyond the disaffected and those with logistical barriers.
"There's a third group," he said. "They just don't connect politics to their lives."
GOTV EFFORTSPolitical organizations on both sides do have get-out-the-vote (GOTV) efforts across the country, including some aimed at first-time and nonvoters.
Conservative groups — such as Christians United for Israel — hope to turn out evangelicals for Trump and Republicans. That includes working with churches across the country on support for Israel and voter mobilization.
Democrats look to college campuses, as well as Native Americans, Blacks and Hispanics in key races.
In Montana, Nick Marroletti, coordinated campaign director for the state Democratic Party, said grassroots turn-out efforts have included knocking on 100,000 doors and making 97,000 phone calls supporting U.S. Sen. Jon Tester, who faces a tough challenge from Republican Tim Sheehy.
'LACK OF FAITH'Mara Ostfeld, a research scientist at the University of Michigan, analyzed voting sentiments in Detroit and found Latino voters, in particular, have lower turnout propensities.
Ostfeld agrees that nonvoters, especially lower-income ones, don't see the outcome of elections impacting their daily lives.
"There is a disconnect," Ostfeld said. But she also said that doesn't mean nonvoters are not engaged or connected to their communities in other ways and don't follow politics.
"It's not like they are disinterested or disengaged," Ostfeld said. "There is just a lack of faith in the political system in particular."

title: Exhibit to show charm and beauty of Delmarva
author: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Exhibit to show charm and beauty of Delmarva

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Arts 
 
 438
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The "Science of Photography" as captured by the artist's eye will be on full display for those who appreciate what is revealed through the camera and life's lens when a new exhibit opens in Chestertown on Wednesday, July 3.The exhibition, which runs through Aug. 28 in the interior public areas of the Heron Point Retirement Community, will display the works of seven talented photographers who have a knack for chronicling the exquisite beauty and inherent charm associated with living in and among the environs and the inhabitants of what is known as the Delmarva.
Barbara Finneson, a representative of Heron Point's Art Interest Group, said she is personally very excited to view the work of this particular collective of artists. "This is a special group," she said, noting that it is based in Salisbury, and includes the works of Mike Morris, Libby Morris, Kenneth Jones, Tony Burton, Latoya Drummond, Samuel Everett and Seldon Dix.
This group of photographic professionals and friends has been known to do whatever it takes, whether that means chasing 3 a.m. sunrises, enduring bitter cold, or patiently waiting for just the right light and conditions to evolve, to get the perfect shot.
"These Delmarva artists," according to the statement provided by the Art Interest Group, "…are dedicated to capturing the unique beauty and essence of Delmarva through their lens. Their collection of work showcases the diverse landscapes, vibrant communities, and rich cultural heritage of the region, applying their individual perspectives and artistic styles. They create a fresh and innovative approach to documenting the natural wonders and human stories of Maryland's Eastern Shore."
Finneson, who is a 20-year resident of Heron Point, said her community always has the good fortune to have artistic works on display in its common areas by talented resident artists and others from the community at-large. Heron Point residents, she said, are oftentimes so inspired by what they see in these exhibitions, they have been known to start painting for the first time at the age of 80, and they particularly look forward to these special collections.
While the opening will take place on July 3 at 10 a.m., the artists themselves will be on-hand for a special gathering on the afternoon on Sunday, July 14 from 2 to 4 p.m. to speak to visitors about their creative process. The community is encouraged to come and participate in the discussion.
This exhibition will be open to the public daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. from June 3 through Aug. 28, with many works available for purchase. Heron Point of Chestertown is located at 501 East Campus Avenue, Chestertown. Call 410-778-7300 for more information.

title: Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 2164
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It wasn't a prediction.It was just something Mike Kern believed.
"If we can get out of the region, I think we have a good shot at states," Kern said of Queen Anne's County High's girls soccer team.
That was at the outset of the season. The Lions did get out of the region, then went on to become the first Bayside Conference school ever to win a girls state soccer championship.
Now, as the girls basketball season approaches tip-off, Kern again strongly believes if Queen Anne's can get out of its region, it has a chance to do well at the state level.
"We're very multi-dimensional," Kern said. "All of our guards can penetrate and shoot. And then our post players are very dangerous inside. They move well. They're very athletic. So I think the sky's the limit for them. The biggest thing is play as a team. We learned that in soccer. If we play as a team and aren't selfish, and do the little things, I think we can do really well."
Getting out of the Class 2A East Region II could prove more difficult than in soccer. Kent Island still has Sydney Riska and Lacey Dauses. Wicomico returns the bulk of the team that handed the Lions their only three losses last season, including bouts for the Bayside Conference and 2A East Region II championships. And Parkside has improved.
But this Queen Anne's team is different.
Not only does Kern return the majority of a team that went 20-3 and won the North Bayside championship, he welcomes two additions who have the potential to be impact players in juniors Damya Henry, a transfer from Cambridge-South Dorchester, and Cheyanne Hollis — daughter of Queen Anne's boys head coach Jeff Hollis — who has been sidelined by injury the past two seasons.
"With our core coming back, plus those additions, I think we stand a good chance of challenging them this year," Kern said of Wicomico. "Damya gives us that defensive pressure. She reads well. Anticipates well. And she's quick. So she definitely helps on the defensive end.
"And Chayenne, she's a true post player; and that will free up Bea (Holthaus) and Lucy (Taylor) a little bit having her in there," Kern continued.
Then there's the core group. Seniors RJ Ensor and Lucy Taylor return along with sophomores Laila Coles, Kariana Hickson, and Holthaus, the 2023 North Bayside Player of the Year.
"The thing about our team right now, I feel like we can score so many different ways," Kern said. "We have pretty good shooters. We can get the ball inside. We can drive. We're a very multi-dimensional team. And Bea herself is very multi-dimensional. She can play outside, go inside. She can drive.
"I'm not worried about us being able to score this year," Kern added. "My biggest focus so far is making sure we play good defense. One of the things that we've done well over the years is we've been a really good defensive team. And I feel like we have so much energy on the offense, that we kind of rest on the defense. And we can't do that with good teams. So we have to play up-tempo defense the entire game."
Kent Island remains Queen Anne's biggest challenger, though Cambridge-SD, with the senior core of Le'Asia Todd, Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin have the potential to give Queen Anne's a battle.
Here's a look at this season's teams.
CAMBRIDGE-SD
Head Coach: Shamya Johnson.
Who's Where: Le'Asia Todd (Sr., C); Destiny Johnson (Sr., G); Tejanae Ballin (Sr., PG); AzEyera Johnson (Sr., F); Skyla Ali (So., F); Jade Ballin (So., F); JaNaya Stanley (Jr., G); Tonyia Brooks (Sr., G); Aamiyah Wilcox (Sr., C); Neveah Adams (Fr., G); Montiasha Jackson (So., G); Amari Winters (Fr., F/C); Kennedy Bourne (So., F); Kamryn Bourne (So., F); D'Asia Mack (So., G).
Outlook: Todd can reach 1,000 career points in Thursday's opener against Crisfield, and together with Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin makes the Vikings a favorite in 1A East Region II.
And though Coach Johnson thinks Cambridge-SD can again reach the 1A state quarterfinals, one of her biggest challenges is keeping her team's intensity and discipline up from start to finish.
"That was the conversation we had tonight,' Coach Johnson said Tuesday in a phone interview. "'You all got it. You've got the pieces. But you all don't have the discipline. And that's the difference.'"
Johnson also knows her team needs to play great transition defense and create points off turnovers if it hopes to challenge Queen Anne's and Kent Island.
COL. RICHARDSON
Head Coach: Tom Corsey.
Who's Where: Jaz Jackson (Jr., G); Monae Ross (Sr., C); Selina Austriville (So., F); Tybria Williams (Sr., G); Ella Downie (So., F); Angelina Algre (Fr., C).
Outlook: Corsey thinks the 6-foot-5 Algre can develop into an inside force.
"She's a work in progress," Corsey said. "She's a presence. She's learning, but I'm going to get her there."
This is one of the younger teams Corsey's coached, but the goal is another 10-win season with eyes on upsetting a 2A school.
EASTON
Head Coach: Lesley Staehli.
Who's Where: Sam Murphy (Sr., G); Serenity Velez (Jr., G); Maia Bailey (Fr., G); Ki'Mauri Lewis (So., G); Jordyn Wilson-Colbert (So., F/C); Myles Booker (Sr., F/C); Dakota Dietrich (Sr., G); Addison Knox (So., G/F); Stella Kabler (Jr., G); Taylor Bowen (Fr., F/C); Addison Chandler (Sr., G/F).
Outlook: The Warriors are an interesting mix.
Velez returns as one of the team's top scorers, and Murphy has transferred from Saints Peter and Paul.
"She is one of the scrappiest people I have ever played against the last four years that I've been coaching defense wise," Staehli said of Murphy. "Now it's awesome to have her with us because she barely comes out."
Bailey, daughter of Marty Bailey, who has come over from the boys team to be an assistant, could be one of the Bayside's top newcomers. And then there is a list of talent that includes Knox, Kabler and Bowen, who helped the Warriors reach the state field hockey semifinals this past season, and Chandler, a force on the Easton soccer team.
"We're going to be fast," Staehli said. "Everybody has talent. I think we're going to shock a lot of people this year with the fact (they're) not expecting a lot of athletic people to come back into the program with us having no jayvee last year. There's certain teams we'll struggle with, but I think we're going to be pretty good."
KENT COUNTY
Head Coach: Tyray Johnson.
Who's Where: Kate Cannon (Sr., C); Talicia Wright (So., PG); Jane Cleary (So., F); Love Jackson (Jr., SF); Kaliyah Smith (Sr., SF); Ariyana Green (So., SF); Saniyah Jones (So., C); Tameeia Savage (Jr., SF); Juliette Camilli (Jr., SG); Sanorra Parker (Fr., SG); Abigael Lachance (Sr., SF); Emerence Boutaud (Jr., PF).
Outlook: Johnson begins his fourth season with the biggest roster he's ever had at Kent with 12. Though still young, experience was gained last year, especially with Wright, who returns at point guard.
"We turned the ball over a lot last year," Johnson said. "She (Wright) stepped up toward the end of the season. So a lot of the mistakes she made early on we won't really have them this year. So it's going to be less turnovers for us."
Speed and defense will be critical if the undersized Trojans are to improve on last season's five-win mark.
KENT ISLAND
Head Coach: Dave Plumer.
Who's Where: Sydney Riska (Sr., F); Lacey Dauses (Jr., G); Abigail Staton (Sr., PG); Ellie Burnside (Sr., G); Machaela Thomas (So., C); Avery Eaton (Sr., G)
Outlook: Lilli Dauses graduated and Makayla Kropfelder transferred to Broadneck. But don't expect the Bucs to fall far from the top.
The smooth-playing Riska was a double-double machine last season, and Lacey Dauses gained confidence with her ability to attack the rim and draw contact. Add Thomas, a 6-foot-2 center, who could create problems for opponents, and Burnside, the first player off the bench from last season.
"I think Lacey had grown as a player and in size," Plumer said. "Obviously Sydney had a big year last year, and now adding another 6-2 center to play along side of her is going to benefit her as well. Who are you going to guard? Machaela's got great footwork. She just needs playing time to get better.
"I think we got to run," Plumer continued. "I mean we're guard heavy. We do have a big player inside but I think we're going to be a running team. We just got to play. There's talent there. It's going to take them a month or two to get them up to speed. But they can play."
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: AJ Jackson.
Who's Where: Taryn Brandt (Sr., G); Jasiyah Henry (Sr., G); Emma Keating (Sr., F); Ashley Kercheval (Sr., F); Megan Rogers (Sr., G); Kaitlyn Thompson (Sr., C); Sarah Brown (Sr., G); MyKira Allen (Jr., F); Yariah Dowell (Jr., G); Irma Sanchez (Jr., G); Nevaeh Irby (So., G).
Outlook: The Bulldogs lost the majority of their scoring from last season with the graduation of Precious Phillips, Chloe Escoe, Ashleigh Lawry and first-team all-North Bayside pick Selaya Garrison.
Jackson will lean heavily on Henry, a four-year varsity starter, for scoring, along with Keating and Dowell.
"Getting back to the fundamentals," Jackson said Caroline's key to success. "Rebounding, boxing out, good passes. The basics. So far I've loved what I've seen in preseason. The girls are buying in. There are some things we need to improve on, but the girls are working hard."
NORTH DORCHESTER
Head Coach: Dontele Pinder.
Who's Where: Remedy Wongus (So., G/F); Areinya Taylor (Sr., G); Ziya Patton (Sr., F); Diamond Newbill (Fr., G); Sammir Holland (Fr., G); Destiny Wongus (Fr., G).
Outlook: An assistant at Colonel Richardson the past eight seasons, Pinder begins his first head coaching job with plenty of optimism.
"I feel like we have a great core group," Pinder said. "We're kind of in the middle of the transition, where we have some of our key seniors that are leading, but we have a good group of freshmen that I feel like are going to be productive in the beginning. I'm excited and I think they're excited about the change. Hopefully we can make some noise here in the North."
QUEEN ANNE'S
Head Coach: Mike Kern.

title: Bay Bridge traffic situation only getting worse
author: MICHAEL SAKATA
content:
Bay Bridge traffic situation only getting worse

 July 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MICHAEL SAKATA | Section: Columns 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Weekends are no longer sustainable on the Eastern Shore. Nor, for that matter, are most weekdays.The 16-mile traffic backups that paralyzed Maryland's Mid-Shore and Upper Shore on July 6, as thousands of weary families spent the waning hours of their holiday weekends languishing on westbound U.S. 50, were unsurprising to those who cross the Bay Bridge and travel this corridor on a regular basis. To their credit, our state and local leaders have used every available Band-Aid to mitigate this crisis — from eliminating the outdated booths at the Bay Bridge's eastbound toll plaza, to closing westbound access roads to weekend through traffic.
Despite their best efforts, though, the situation will only get worse.
As the population of the Eastern Shore continues to climb, regional policymakers work to expand housing inventories in order to meet demand, and the Shore becomes an increasingly popular destination for year-round entertainment and tourism, congestion will only intensify. There will, inevitably, come a time when backups of this magnitude are a daily occurrence and Shore residents are effectively cut off from jobs, emergency services and one another.
Given the inevitability of these trends, and the amount of time it takes for transportation projects to be funded and built in the state of Maryland, we must recognize that the time for action is now. By waiting any longer to commit to a visionary transportation mobility plan, we will only put these Marylanders' lives, livelihoods and quality of life at severe risk.
Given the stakes, Gov. Moore and the Maryland General Assembly are to be commended for committing an additional $500 million to some of our state's most urgent projects this past legislative session. This was a vital first step, but with more than $3 billion in unsatisfied priorities and a statewide network of roads, highways and bridges that continue to crumble with age, it is now time to take a quantum leap forward.
The Maryland Transportation Builders & Materials Association, which represents roughly 240 businesses (and therefore over 100,000 Maryland employees) across the DMV region, has developed a comprehensive regional approach to the U.S. 50 congestion crisis. An approach that recognizes this situation is much bigger than any single project and, therefore, addresses the challenge at multiple chokepoints and safety hazards.
Specifically, our plan calls upon our state leaders to wrap up what has been an interminable Chesapeake Bay Bridge Crossing Study, determine the best strategy for adding significant lane capacity and begin the arduous process of securing the massive funding that will be necessary to move the project forward. We do so, however, knowing that expanded Bay Bridge capacity alone will not solve the problem entirely.
Therefore, we are also calling for action on the following projects — all of which are in the Maryland Department of Transportation's six-year program — and are highlighted in our "25 for 25" campaign. These projects will help our state to meet the demands of the mid-21st century and beyond:
Construction of a grade-separated interchange at U.S. Route 50 and 213 in Wye Mills.Safety improvements at the highly perilous intersection of U.S. 50 and the Easton Bypass.Widening of I-97 to six lanes between U.S. Route 50 and state Route 32.Addition of lane capacity at U.S. Route 50 and Ritchie Highway.Capacity, safety and functionality improvements along the state Route 90 corridor, from U.S. 50 to Coastal Highway.Replacement of the unreliable Sinepuxent Bay drawbridge at the Ocean City Inlet.
To be sure, this is an ambitious plan. In fact, likely the most thorough reimagining of the Eastern Shore's transportation capacity since the "Reach the Beach" program nearly 40 years ago. It is also an expensive ask at a time when our primary sources of transportation revenue are plummeting due to improved gas mileage, reduction in gasoline-powered automobiles and various economic pressures.
However, to suggest that these projects simply cannot be done would imply that they are merely a luxury and not a necessity. As the primary voice of Maryland's transportation industry, we believe that failure to act is no longer an acceptable option. Even in the face of unprecedented fiscal and economic challenges, our elected officials and business leaders must come together — absent the partisan and geographic rivalries that so often act as impediments to progress — and determine how, and not if, we will make this vision a reality.
We simply cannot continue to live like this.

title: Trappe Council introduces ordinance to raise water and sewer usage fees
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe Council introduces ordinance to raise water and sewer usage fees

 May 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 381
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Council introduced an ordinance to raise water and sewer usage fees.The introduction of Ordinance 3-2024 would amend section 14 of the Trappe Town Code to increase the water and sewer monthly fees for usage.
The monthly water usage rate is $4.70 per 1,000 gallons, and it's being proposed that it go to $6.20 per 1,000. The monthly sewer usage rate is currently $10.98 per 1,000, and it is proposed that it go to $11.48 per 1,000.
The base fees would not be increased, but the usage fees would be. Commissioner Brian Schmidt, council president, said that though the council does not like to increase fees, the town is in "desperate" need of it.
Schmidt said Trappe currently has three pumping stations that need repair, which would cost roughly $3 million. He also added that Trappe has a $13 million wastewater treatment plant that also needs repairs.
"While we hate to increase rates, the financial stability of the town is kind of in need of it," Schmidt said.
Additionally, the council approved introducing Ordinance 2-2024, adopting the FY2025 budget. This budget established a property tax rate of 33 cents per $100 of assessed real property value and 75 cents per $100 on commercial or business, personal property or public utility.
It also established an annual fee of $182 per residential household for trash collection service and adopted an enterprise budget for the town's water and sewer operations.
Erin Braband, Trappe administrator, pointed out that the tax rate for assessed real property and business personal property is not increasing, and the trash rate is not increasing.
Finally, the council approved the transfer of wastewater allocation from six lots in the Lakeside at Trappe development to the community pool for Lakeside residents.
Lakeside has purchased 120 units and issued 114 permits for homes to be built. The remaining six lots will go toward the community pool.
"We're transferring the sewer allocation from those six lots to the community center lots, so there's sewer allocation for the restrooms in the community center," Attorney Ryan Showalter said. "And this agreement basically says we're not going to build houses on those lots for occupancy, we're not gonna open anything for occupancy until the new treatment plant is open."
The council unanimously approved the agreement for wastewater allocation and development restrictions.

title: Pastoral Ponderings: Replacing fear with love
author: KEN GEORGE Ridgely Church of the Bretheren
content:
Pastoral Ponderings: Replacing fear with love

 May 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KEN GEORGE Ridgely Church of the Bretheren | Section: Columns 
 
 277
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There are many scriptures that tell us to "fear the Lord." My early Christian experiences certainly taught me that. I remember a pamphlet that showed sinners drowning in a literal lake of fire for all eternity. Scary stuff.Author and pastor Rob Bell presents us with an interesting thought though — do we really believe that God, who loves us so much, is going to condemn billions of people, and reward only a select few with heaven? Will He really condemn these billions, throughout history, with eternal torment for things they did in a few short years of their life on Earth? It's not a question I would presume to know the answer to.
I do know this, just as well as you do — our God is a God of love. He loves us so much that He gave His only begotten Son. Therefore, I prefer to substitute "fear" with "love." For instance, Proverbs 1:7 tells us, "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. Fools despise wisdom and instruction." I like to think that "the love of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge."
I must admit, I have no fear of the Lord. Instead, what I have is respect, reverence, awe, love and an appreciation of His love for me. The love He shows us cannot not be compared to anything else. The angels who appeared to the shepherds, in the Gospel of Luke, gave us good advice: "Don't be afraid, because a savior is born."
Jesus came to us — God in the flesh — bringing love and salvation.
If we live a life of righteousness, following Christ, what do we have to fear? Nothing.

title: A defining moment in Congress
author: Staff Writer
content:
A defining moment in Congress

 October 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox

 Welcome back to Washington, Andy Harris, for the start of the legislative session. I trust your recess was restful. Unfortunately, it was also silent. You chose not to hold a town hall meeting during your time in the district. That absence did not go unnoticed. It deprived your constituents of the chance to hear you explain why you reversed yourself on the spending bill you had so fiercely opposed — until you suddenly didn't. You claimed "assurances" persuaded you. Assurances of what, exactly? Your vote helped push through the single largest increase in the federal deficit in history. If you stand by that decision, you should have had the courage to face us and defend it.But my main concern today is not the budget, it is the Jeffrey Epstein files. You are a Catholic. You are a father of daughters. Given both, it should not require any moral calculus to condemn not only Epstein, but also anyone who willingly associated with him while he and his circle exploited, abused, and demeaned young women. The conduct in question — sexual assault, abuse of minors, harassment in dressing rooms, grotesque violations of trust — is abhorrent. And participation in, or willful blindness to, these acts is unforgivable.
Your colleagues in Congress are circulating a bipartisan discharge petition demanding the release of all Epstein files. This is a defining moment for you. Will you align yourself with justice and transparency, or will you shield predators and the powerful? As a father, you owe this to every parent whose child was harmed. As a man of faith, you owe it to your conscience. As my representative, you owe it to me.
So let me be clear: I expect you to sign this petition. I demand that you sign it. Your record of retreat and equivocation has already earned you the nickname "nowhere man." If you fail to step up here, it will confirm that title — and worse, it will mark you as someone who turned away from the helpless in their moment of need.
The victims deserve closure. The public deserves the truth. The perpetrators deserve justice. Representative Harris, history will remember whether you stood tall or disappeared. Choose wisely.
DAN McKEW
Easton

title: Hispanic Heritage Month celebrated in Kent County
content:
Hispanic Heritage Month celebrated in Kent County

 October 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 1 | Section: News

 CHESTERTOWN - The lilting chorus of Cuban folk song "Guantanamera" filled the cafeteria of H.H.Garnet Elementary School in Chestertown Thursday, Sept. 21.Local resident and artist Fredy Granillo strummed his guitar as he taught the song to students that morning as part of the Celebración del mes del la Herencia Hispana in the county.The Celebration of Hispanic Heritage Month was brought into schools during September through partnerships with the Kent County Local Management Board and the Kent Cultural Alliance.The two organizations were joined by others in holding a variety of community events including art programs and a block party centered around Hispanic heritage."The Kent Cultural Alliance was honored to work with the Kent County Local Management Board and E(Ñ)E: Alianza para la Cultura y Comunidad Hispana, to create a month long celebration of the contributions of Kent County's Latino community," said John Schratwieser, executive director of the Kent Cultural Alliance."Celebrating those who contribute so much to our economic health and our quality of life, and doing that through art, music, food, dance and the written word, is paramount to the mission of the KCA." For Granillo, who also is a Kent County Public Schools parent, getting to share his family's cultural touchstones with students is a valuable experience.Granillo grew up in El Salvador. He and his wife Kent County Local Management Board Director Rosemary Ramsey Granillo moved to Chestertown when their son, a fourth grader at Garnet, was 2.Granillo found the community friendly and inviting, but he still faced hurdles - first being the language.He learned English and he helped his son with the language.There were additional cultural differences for Granillo as well, such as food, and he sees other families having similar experiences when they move here."I was lucky because I had the opportunity to visit Chestertown first," Granillo said. "So I knew about the artistic community in town and that was something that made me feel like I could live here." For students who move to Kent County from other countries, school can pose a big challenge.Beyond learning math standards, science, social studies and other subjects, they also have a new language to learn - and Kent County Public Schools has staff members dedicated to helping those English language learners.Granillo said programs like Hispanic Heritage Month are important for both students born and raised here and those who have moved to the area from other countries.It gives those students from other countries an opportunity and a space to share their culture with their new peers.Granillo spoke about how celebrations in other countries are often built around specific foods, activities and games - not unlike the American custom of eating turkey on Thanksgiving."I think it's really important for schools to have a space where these kids can show other kids what they like to do in their countries, because that gives you a perspective on the world," he said."When you are a kid, you need to understand the world is more than Chestertown or the town where you live." As part of Hispanic Heritage Month in Kent County Public Schools, there were lessons and school announcements teaching students about the culture.Galena Elementary School, for example, held a daily Hispanic Heritage contest, with questions that students could answer by looking at information posted throughout the building.Teacher Tracey Kendall-Parent works with local English language learners in Galena Elementary School. She took to the morning announcements throughout the month to provide information about countries where students' families are from."I think that's a beautiful experience for everybody, not just for the kids," Granillo said of the Hispanic heritage lessons. "And it's going to make these kids from other countries feel like they live in a space where they can celebrate their culture and their identity too."

title: R & B Singer Rudolph Isley dies at age 84
content:
R & B Singer Rudolph Isley dies at age 84

 Rudolph Isley, a founding member of the Isley Brothers who helped perform such raw rhythm and blues classics as "Shout" and "Twist and Shout" and the funky hits "That Lady" and "It's Your Thing," has died at age 84."There are no words to express my feelings and the love I have for my brother. Our family will miss him. But I know he's in a better place," Ronald Isley said in a statement released Thursday by an Isley Brothers publicist.Further details were not immediately available.A Cincinnati native, Rudolph Isley began singing in church with brothers Ronald and O'Kelly (another sibling, Vernon, died at age 13) and was still in his teens when they broke through in the late 1950s with "Shout," a secularized gospel rave that was later immortalized during the toga party scene in "Animal House." The Isleys scored again in the early 1960s with the equally spirited "Twist and Shout," which the Beatles liked so much they used it as the closing song on their debut album and opened with it for their famed 1965 concert at Shea Stadium.The Isleys' other hits included "This Old Heart of Mine (Is Weak for You)," later covered by Rod Stewart, and the Grammy-winning "It's Your Thing." In the 1970s, after younger brother Ernest and Marvin joined the group, they had even greater success with such singles as "That Lady" and "Fight the Power (Part 1)" and such million-selling albums as "The Heat Is On" and "Go for Your Guns." Rudolph Isley left the group in 1989, three years after the sudden death of O'Kelly Isley, to become a Christian minister. He was among the Isleys inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1992.

 On May 24, 1935, the first Major League Baseball game to be played at night took place at Cincinnati's Crosley Field as the Reds beat the Philadelphia Phillies, 2-1.On this date:

In 1961, a group of Freedom Riders was arrested after arriving at a bus terminal in Jackson, Mississippi, charged with breaching the peace for entering white-designated areas. (They ended up serving 60 days in jail.)
In 1962, astronaut Scott Carpenter became the second American to orbit the Earth as he flew aboard Aurora 7.
In 1974, American jazz composer and bandleader Duke Ellington, 75, died in New York.

In 1980, Iran rejected a call by the World Court in The Hague to release the American hostages.

title: One proves enough for Easton
author: Bill Haufe
content:
One proves enough for Easton

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 568

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Both coaches obviously wanted victory, and after 80 minutes of heated, physical play in the latest installment of the Easton-St. Michaels High soccer rivalry, Warrior head coach Avery Brice breathed a sigh of relief as his team continued its late-season surge."Good game. One-oh. Got the result," Brice said after Rodrigo Fresco's goal in the fifth minute Wednesday night proved enough for a 1-0 Easton victory over the Saints.
And though St. Michaels suffered its fourth loss in five games, Saints head coach Pat Hambleton may have gotten something he was looking for as well — momentum.
"We've had a hard stretch," Hambleton said after his team's third one-goal loss in 10 days, which included a 3-2 double-overtime defeat to two-time defending North Bayside champion Queen Anne's County. "I asked them, 'Just give us momentum. Create momentum so we can move forward. Win, lose, draw, figure out a way to play well. Work hard. Find something to carry on for tomorrow (a 9-0 victory Thursday over Cambridge-South Dorchester) and then carry on into the playoffs.'"
The Saints (6-4-1 overall, 2-4-1 North Bayside) may have found that momentum, playing the game's last 35 minutes, 54 seconds a man down after one of its players received a red card while an Easton player was given a yellow.
"I thought down (to) 10 men, I felt like we had the upper hand, and I felt like we were the man up," said Hambleton, who argued Easton should have also received a red.
"Couldn't be more proud," Hambleton added of his team. "We took them out of their game. They were sitting six guys in the back for the last 20 minutes terrified of our attack and our pressure. And I thought the second half was a completely different game than the first half."
With 4:28 elapsed in the first half, Fresco got a ball on the right side and parked it past Saints keeper Lucas Greenwood for the game's lone goal and a 1-0 Warrior lead.
The remainder of the game featured a string of highlight-reel saves by Greenwood (10 saves) and Easton goalie Sam Hutchison (eight saves).
Greenwood leaped to punch a ball away with 26:10 remaining in the first half. Hutchison stopped St. Michaels' Abel Delgaudio just 50 seconds later. Greenwood lunged left to foil Luke Stanco a little over 5 minutes later. St. Michaels' Connor Wheeler then struck a direct kick that Hutchison reached before colliding with Delgaudio. Greenwood made another stop a moment later, and Hutchsion responded with another save before a second collision 5 minutes later, leaving Brice pleading with his team, "You need to wake up."
The game was mostly played between the 18s in the second half, though both keepers continued to come up big. Easton had a chance to pad its lead 9 minutes into the half, but Emmet Fox drove a shot off the left post. Hutchison picked up another save, when he knocked away a ball on a Saints corner. Greenwood maintained the one-goal difference, smothering a ball off a wild scramble with an Easton player leaping over him.
"We just need to be consistent in the back and then take care of the ball a little bit better," said Brice, his team 6-5, 6-2 after its fourth win in five games.
For Hambleton, it was a familiar theme.
"The story of the second half of our season is we're winning games off the scoreboard," Hambleton said. "And that doesn't count."

title: Community celebrates Earth Day at Adkins Arboretum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Community celebrates Earth Day at Adkins Arboretum

 April 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Swinging jazz, food, ecology and crafts for kids marked the outdoor Earth Day celebration on Saturday at Adkins Arboretum. There was also bird song from the woods and the sound of bullfrogs from the pond.The crowd was large, with 300 tickets sold for the event. Multiple environmental groups and government agencies hosted information tables.
Eastern Redbud saplings were given out for attendees to plant at home by Francis Smith of the Maryland Forest Service. There were master gardeners and monarch butterfly experts. A birding trip led into the forest in the morning.
"Earth Day heightens our awareness and appreciation. It is joyful and good to get out. And it is fun to host this site to share with other local nonprofits," said Ginna Tiernan, executive director of Adkins.
"It reminds us to breathe, step out in nature. It is incredible for your soul, your brain," Tiernan said. "It is amazing how clear you can think after a walk in the woods. I took a walk the other day, and a pileated woodpecker just swooped down in front of me. There were pine warblers in my ear. It is just affirming too that we are here on Earth with all of these animals, and we are a part of them."
Adkins celebrated the global holiday a little early this year, with Earth Day actually falling on Monday.
Earth Day is an annual event on April 22 to demonstrate support for environmental protection. First held on April 22, 1970, it now includes a wide range of events coordinated globally.
Jay Falstad, Adkins Arboretum board member and Executive Director of Queen Anne's Conservation Association, was using yellow and orange chalk to create a big sun at the arboretum's entrance.
"Earth Day is the one thing that we all share. We all share the same air, water and the same planet. We should all have an investment in protecting it," Falstad said.
There were many people who have worked hard to make this event happen. Not just organizing and planning but executing a fun educational experience.
Jenny Houghton, assistant director of Adkins Arboretum, said, "We are partnering with other environmental organizations. We thought it would be nice to show people that we are all working together. We have Pickering Creek, Tuckahoe State Park, Maryland DNR, Bartlett Tree Experts, Shore Rivers, Talbot County Master Gardeners and Phillips Wharf Environmental Center."
"The highlight is getting people outside to celebrate nature together and listening to great music, eating local food and hopefully scooping up some tadpoles in the wetland. It is good to remind ourselves that the Earth is worth taking care of, because it is all that we have got," said Houghton.

title: Deepening Divides - Democrats Split Over 'Anti-Zionism Is Antisemitism' Measure; Poll Shows U.S. Racial, Generational Differences Over Israel-Hamas War
content:
Deepening Divides - Democrats Split Over 'Anti-Zionism Is Antisemitism' Measure; Poll Shows U.S. Racial, Generational Differences Over Israel-Hamas War

 December 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 The U.S. House of Representatives approved a measure Wednesday declaring that "anti-Zionism is antisemitism" prompting a split among Democrats.A majority of House Democrats did not vote for the measure as a public opinion poll from Gallup shows substantial divides among Americans over the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza by age, race and political persuasion.
Whites, older voters and Republicans tend to back Israel in its war against Hamas after the Oct. 7 terror attacks while younger Americans, people of color and Democrats disapprove of Israel's air strikes and ground invasion of Gaza aimed at the Islamic militant group, according to a poll released Nov. 30 by Gallup.
The congressional measure condemning antisemitism passed with support from 216 Republicans and 95 Democrats. The resolution's most controversial component was plank equating anti-Zionism with antisemitism.
Zionism is a movement and belief system that supports the Jewish state of Israel in the Middle East.
"Zionism is the movement for the self-determination and statehood for the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland, the land of Israel," according to the Anti-Defamation League.
Thirteen Democrats voted against the measure and 105 Dems voted 'present' or did not vote neither supporting nor opposing the resolution.
One Republican - U.S.
Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky - voted against the anti-Zionism/antisemitism measure. Another four GOP lawmakers did not vote.
"Anti-Zionism isn't antisemitism," Massie said in a social media statement pointing to congressional remarks by U.S. Rep. Jerrold Nadler, D-New York, that some Orthodox and other Jews are not in agreement with modern Zionist constructs.
Nadler, the House's most senior Jewish members, said some Orthodox Jews believe only the Messiah can establish a new state of Israel and the measure can label progressive Jews and others critical of controversial judicial reforms in Israel as antisemitic.
Nadler and U.S. House Majority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, were among those voting present on antisemitism measure.
The 13 Democratic no votes came from progressives who have been critical of Israel's war in Gaza against Hamas and U.S. support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the Islamic militant group's Oct. 7 attacks.
Opponents of the measure - which referenced rises antisemitic vandalism and violence - included U.S. Reps. Jamaal Bowman and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota and Pramila Jayapal of Washington "We must be steadfast and clear in condemning antisemitism. The extreme GOP resolution on the floor today had no Democratic cosponsors and inappropriately said all anti-Zionism is antisemitism. Muddying the waters about what antisemitism is, is completely wrong and unhelpful," said Jayapal who had to clarify recent comments about whether she condemned Hamas' rapes and violence against women and girls in the Oct. 7.
GOP SUPPORTS MEASURE U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican representing the Eastern Shore, voted for the antisemitism measure along with Maryland Democratic U.S. Reps.
Steny Hoyer, David Trone, Dutch Ruppersberger and Kweisi Mfume. Maryland Democratic U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin and John Sarbanes voted present.
House Republicans overwhelmingly backed the resolution which labels some pro-Palestinian slogans as antisemitic.
"More Jews were murdered on October 7th than on any other single day since the Holocaust.
Let that sink in. We have even seen members of this very body repeat blatantly antisemitic rhetoric and spread lies about Israel and her right to exist. Let me be absolutely clear: such hate has no place in the halls of Congress nor our national discourse. It is our fundamental responsibility as leaders and Members of Congress to condemn and fight these horrific acts of hate and discrimination against the Jewish community," said U.S. Rep. David Kustoff, R-Tennessee, one of the main sponsors of the resolution.
GOP backers of the measure point to a rise in antisemitic incidents and pro-Hamas and pro-Palestinian rhetoric that calls for or insinuates the destruction of Israel. They also point to the 106 no or present that did not support the measure - 105 of them from Democrat.
"The world has seen a drastic rise of antisemitism since October 7th that is deeply disheartening and extremely concerning," said U.S. Max Miller, R-Ohio. "Elected leaders must have the courage to condemn and fight all forms of domestic and global antisemitism.
While I am glad this resolution passed the House today, I am disappointed that 106 of my colleagues failed to take this opportunity to condemn antisemitism forcefully." AMERICA DIVIDED The Gallup poll released Nov. 30 shows significant splits over the Holy Land war by race, political party and gender.
The polls shows 71% of Republicans back Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza versus support from 36% of Democrats.
Fifty nine percent of men approve of Israel's war in Gaza versus 44% of women, according the Gallup Among people of color, 64% disapprove of Israel's attacks against Hamas in Gaza while 61% of whites backs Netanyahu's efforts to dismantle the militant group.
There is a similar split my age with 67% of younger Americans (ages 18 to 34) disapproving of Israel's war against Hamas and 63% of voters 55 and older backing the Israel Defense Forces' military effort.
Palestinian health authorities in Hamas-controlled Gaza say more than 17,000 people have died since Holy Land war stared in October Israeli officials say Hamas fighters killed more than 1,200 people and took more than 240 hostages in the Oct. 7 terror attacks.

 CAMBRIDGE — A Delaware man has been arrested by Cambridge police on drug charges after allegedly striking a person — who police say appeared to be suffering from an overdose — with a vehicle before leaving the scene.Justin Cannon, 34, of Seaford, Delaware, was arrested on July 5, charged with a felony count of controlled dangerous substance possession with intent to distribute a narcotic drug and three misdemeanor counts of controlled dangerous substance possession.
He faces seven traffic citations, according to a Cambridge Police Department press release.
Just before 3:30 p.m. on July 5, police responded to the 500 block of Muir Street. Police say they found a female possibly suffering from a drug overdose. She was flown to Shock Trauma, police said.
Investigators determined the female victim was left in that area and "struck by the vehicle as it left," the press release stated.
Later that evening, police located the suspected vehicle driven by Cannon. With the help of the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office K-9 unit, police say they found individually packaged heroin in the vehicle.
After Cannon was arrested, police said he acknowledged involvement.
"Cannon admitted to being with the female victim and hitting the subject with his vehicle," the press release stated.
Cannon is being held at the Dorchester County Department of Corrections on no bond, police said. A preliminary hearing for the four drug charges is slated for July 21.

title: Stepping into the past - Museum explores Tubman's life through murals
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Stepping into the past - Museum explores Tubman's life through murals

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 941
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In the back of the Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center on Race Street, one wall acts as a window into Tubman's life.Inside the museum, on one side of the wall, Tubman is painted as a young girl, about 13-years-old, at the Bucktown General Store.
"This was a pivotal time in her life," Linda Harris, the museum's director of events and docent, said. "It was considered her first act of defiance." Outside the museum, on the other side of the wall, Tubman is an adult, holding out her hand.
"(She's) coming back, rescuing family and those that wanted freedom," artist of both murals, Michael Rosato said.
Harriet Tubman, an abolitionist and social activist who was born into and escaped from slavery in Dorchester County in the 19th century, became well-known for her work on the Underground Railroad, a network of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape to their freedom.
Inside the museum, the mural of a young Tubman and the Bucktown Store covers the entire wall - and the other three walls in the room.
With canvas and paint, Rosato has transformed the back room of the museum into the Bucktown Store, a significant place in Tubman's history.
The story goes that Tubman was asked to go to the Bucktown Store to get something for the master.
"And she didn't want to do it," Bill Jarmon, president of the Harriet Tubman Organization, said.
"Part of it had to do with the fact that she wasn't presentable." It had to do with her hair, Jarmon said. So she covered her hair with a cloth made from flaxseed.
When Tubman got to the store, she heard a noise at the backdoor and saw a young boy struggling to get away from his master. When the boy escapes and runs toward the door, Tubman is told to stop him. But she doesn't. She steps out of the way to let him go through. "Her first act of defiance," as Harris said.
As the boy escaped, Jarmon said, a two-pound weight was thrown at him.
However, the weight hit Tubman in the forehead instead, knocking her unconscious.
Harris considers Tubman's head wrap to be a very important piece of this story.
"She wraps her head in this linen made of flaxseed, which in fact - what I'm reading and what I believe now - cushions the blow from that two-pound weight being hurled at her," Harris said.
"Imagine if she had fixed her hair that day. She'd be dead." Sitting in the back room of the museum Wednesday, Dec. 20, Jarmon and Harris pointed to different parts of the room as they told the story. When they officially open this part of the museum - which they hope to do in January - visitors will feel even more immersed in the story.
They plan to put in wood floors and counters to resemble the store. And as they tell the story of Tubman's first act of defiance, Harris said she and her husband will play code songs, songs enslaved people used to share messages.
Eventually, Harris hopes to offer virtual reality goggles to visitors when they enter the room.
"We're going to make this thing come alive," she said.
The idea to do this all started when Harris learned that she would no longer be able to take visitors on tours inside the original Bucktown Store.
Harris said that considering how pivotal the store was in Tubman's life, she couldn't have people visit and not learn the story.
"So I said, 'Well, let's put it in the museum,'" Harris said.
To begin the project, Rosato, who lives in Church Creek and has been an artist for 33 years, went to the store and took photos of the walls.
"Every square inch of the walls and what was on the shelves," he said.
After that, he took the photos back to his studio on Race Street and put paint to canvas.
"(I) just started to recreate the store as close as possible and in a somewhat realistic fashion so when you're in that space you feel as though you can take things off the shelves," he said.
After completing each wall on the canvas, he would bring the canvases to the museum and glue them to the walls so that it looked as if he had painted directly on walls of the museum. To make it look as realistic as possible, Rosato had to consider light, shadow and perspective.
"When you create a painting that you want to look real and dimensional, you have to understand perspective and find the right vanishing point," he said.
"So when you're standing right in the middle of that room, every wall you look at, all the lines converge to a certain point. And that's what gives it a sense of depth." The project, which Rosato worked on in the fall, took between one and two months to complete.
He said that once it is open to visitors, he hopes they will get a sense of the rich history of Tubman's experience in Dorchester County.
"The possibility of being able to stand there and reflect back like, 'I'm in the store where she is.
This is what happened,'" he said. "And then going outside and seeing (adult) Harriet Tubman. This is the outcome."

Contractor bringing Oxford's Strand project up to specifications

 April 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 OXFORD — Efforts to complete the first phase of the Strand Beach project are underway this week after it was determined the project was not finished to the specifications originally presented to the town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting March 25, Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said work to complete the project would begin the week of March 31.
In order to finish the first phase of the project, the contractor, Underwood and Associates, will lower the islands on the beach, remove temporary access to the islands, purchase and install native plantings and install a grassy strip along the roadway to prevent sand from flowing into the roadway, Wahl said. All of these items are to be completed to match the approved permit and site plan.
Wahl said Underwood and Associates is required to complete this phase of the project by April 19.
In December, the Commissioners of Oxford announced that although the Strand Beach project was signed off on in June by previous Town Manager Cheryl Lewis, the project had not been completed to the specifications that Underwood and Associates had originally presented.
The plan for the project was to create a berm, place hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to bring in sand, create small islands in the water to reduce waves coming onto the beach and plant low marsh grasses on those islands. During the commissioners meeting in December, Commissioner Katrina Greer said not all the grasses had been planted on the islands and the islands were two feet higher in elevation than they were supposed to be.
That month, Greer brought together the Maryland Department of the Environment, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Underwood and Associates and the organizations that funded the project to ensure Underwood and Associates would bring down the elevation of the islands and take out the sand that goes out to the headlands at no cost to the town.
